LONDON, January Lord Kitchener,
telegraphing from Johannesburg Monday,
January 6, reports the occurrence of a
number of skirmishes in various parts of
the war field. The most serious were at
Amersfoort January 3 and January 4, when
Maj. w. H. p. Plomer and Col j. Speus
were in contact with Commandant Chris
tan Botha's and Commandant Opperman's
commands. They drove the Beers from
their positions after considerable fighting.
during which the Somerset Light Infantry
suffered severely. Major Vallentin and
eighteen men were killed and five officers
and twenty-eight men were wounded. The
Beers left nine men dead on the field.
Il Col Colenbrander surprised Field Cornet
Lcuw's laager at Watervale January ;. kill
ing five men and capturing twenty-nfne.
Lord Kitchener mentions other minor sur-
prises and captures.


General French reports that the Beers in
Cape Colony are so reduced in numbers as
to require only an elaborate police system
to keep them in check


The weeks totals of Boer casualties are
36 men killed, 8 wounded, 261 made pris-
oners and 12 surrendered.

Two elaborately carved tombstones have
been completed and placed over the graves
of Naezan and Chiko San, the pair of Jap
anese spaniels whom Miss Daisy Letter
some dogs were the gift of her brother
Joseph Letter. Both died in April of this
year, and were buried with great ceremony
at Linden Lodge, the Lake Geneva, Ill,
home Of the Letters. Prince Naezan the
elder, was Miss Letters favorite. Prince
ling was his pet name, and the whole
Letter household Joined in Miss Letters
worship of her canine friend. When the
silky brown creature with red eyes and a
knot in his tail passed into the great un-
known on April IA there was great grief
and lamentation in the Letter household.
Six days later his playmate, Chiko San,
died, supposedly of grief over the loss of
his elder brother.


The bodies Of the dogs were borne from
the washington mansion, where they died,
to the Geneva home and planted in a little
mound protected by weeping Willows and
there they rest not unknown or unsung,
for every morning during the recent So
journ of the family at Linden Lodge their
double grave was daily covered with mig
nonette and sweet william. Now two
costly tombstones have been erected over
the graves of the animals. The tombstones
are constructed of white marble, and lie
upon the grass like sarcophagi They are
three feet long, two feet wide and about a
foot in height. Besides being elaborately
carved about the sides with all the skill of
the stone cutters art, each is engraved on
the face with the name of the decea sed

Many years ago, perhaps three centuries.
large sailing ship left one of the ports in
old England, bound for the Philippines The
cruise was to last at least ten months and
probably longer. The hold was well filled

goods being carried for the purpose OF

afcnlpeago, who were then living in
savage state, with the exception, perhaps,

century had come in contact with the Span.
iards. To man the ship was a crew of near.
ly 100 hearty men from the British Isle,
some of them old salts who had followed
the sea all their lives, while others were on
their first trip. For the old-timers each
new day tnat set in seemed like the first
while 10 those who had left their homes
for the first time to make trip of so many
months each day grew longer and more
lonesome. AT the end of several months the
beautiful green islands of the Philipnines
were sighted and finally the ship was cruis.
ing along the coast of what Is now Mndoro,
out unknown in those early days.


Trading With Natives.


Several stops were made. boats being sent
ashore and the men doing some trading with
the natives receiving for their goods gold,
pearls and valuable wood. The natives who
are now known the ''Manguianes"
treated the sailors very nicely. being very
hospltable. The vessel sailed around the
island for days. the crew little thinking
OF the typhoon being prepared for them
above.


Finally, one dark night, a storm broke out
which took away spars, rigging and every
movable thing from the deck. At daylight
the next morning the vessel was upon the
shore, q total wreck.


All the crew safely landed ashore In
small boats, carrying with them food. All
that day and several others they stood
upon the shore keeping lookout for any
passing ship, but not a single one or any
single sign Of habitation could be seen.
l. was water before them and the tropical
jungles at their backs.


A town (Sablayan) has since been built
anu marks the memorable spot.

arate villages and maintain their tribe
name, the whites being called Batanes

one from Northwest Europe. the other
from Northeast Asia-mainly by land con-

Monthly" for March. Owing to this sub
stance. which converted the New World

Hence what they have in common with

during the migration period, and that
amounts TO very little-the forms of the
stone implements found amongst all
primitive races; perhaps the frc-drill.

germs of articulate speech, the family
group inherited from the higher anthro-

in the direction of Shamanism; possibly

and swastika, and the rude beginnings
of the simpler arts.

When the fading bowers and slow drop
ping leaves proclaim that the season OF
mist and mellow fruitfulness is here, the
housewife takes a careful inventory of the
stock of good things she has stored in her
preserve closet to make quite sure she has
all the favorite preserves, jelies, jams,
pickles, etc, that will please the palates Of
the different members of her family when
desolate winter succeeds kindly autumns
glorious plenty.


Except for the apple trees which for some
time yet will be filled with fruit, russell and
scarlet and yellow and ripe to the core,
most of our summer products from tree and
vine will soon be touched with autumn's
earliest frost and if not killed outright will
ripen slowly and imperfectly at best. The
first frosts are apt to come while the
tomato vines are stin laden with well-de-
Veloped, but green fruit, and in order to
save these from the frost-blight one may
resort to numerous ways and means. Those
who grow their own vines may take them
up root and branch, providing they have
rather dark and not too dry cellar. Hang
the vines up by the roots the vines will
not touch the ground. In many farm
house cellar vines filled with fine green to-
matoes have been treated in this manner

One usually associates green tomatoes with
pickles only, but while these are the COM
monest variety of pickles, there are other
ways of utilizing them.


Fried Green Tomatoes-No. 1.


Select smooth. round tomatoes of uni
form size; cut them in thin slices and sprin-
kle with salt. Make a fritter batter with
flour, water egg, butter, pepper and salt.
Dip each slice of tomato into the batter,
then fry in sufficient hot fat to brown both
sides at once. Nice for breakfast served
with crisp bacon or poached eggs.


Fried Green Tomatoes-No. 2.


Wipe six large green tomatoes with a
damp cloth, cut them into slices an eighth
of an inch thick, sprinkle the tomatoes with
salt and let them stand a few minutes, then
press out the juice, dust the slices with a
little pepper and sugar or a little ground
ginger; then dip the slices in fine bread
crumbs, then into beaten egg. then again in
the crumbs. Saute them in butter or drip
ping and serve with gravy made fol-
lows: Rub two level tablespoonfuls of but
ter with two of flour to a smooth paste,
then put into a saucepan and stir until
brown; then add a cup of good meat stock
or milk and stir until it thickens; season

Green Tomato Pie.


Peel and cut green tomatoes in thick
slices, then wash in several waters to re-
move most of the seeds. Drop in hot water
and bring to boil then drain off. To each
pound of tomatoes add three-quarters of a
pound of sugar and the grated rind of a
lemon. Cook all together until thick and
tomatoes are clear, then set aside to get
cold Add the juice of lemon and bake in
with bottom crust and stripe of pastry
laid across the top like lattice work.


Green Tomato and Meat Pie.


Slice green tomatoes thin and cover with
boiling salted water; parboil them fifteen
minutes; drain. Butter a baking dish and
put in layer of the tomatoes, then season
with salt; cover with layer Of cold meat
sliced thin, season with salt, pepper and
little table sauce; cover with a layer of
very thin slices of buttered bread; then
more tomatoes, and SO on until dish is fuil
having the top covered with buttered bread
crumbs Pour a little beaten egg over the
top and bake until nice brown.


Preserved Green Tomatoes.


Take small green tomatoes, wash, cover
with boiling water and scald until the skins
loosen; then peel and drain. Take equal
weight of graduated sugar and make a
syrup with water and the juice of a lemon
and few bits of stick cinnamon. Put in the
tomatoes and cook gently until they are
tender and clear. Instead of the cinnamon,
green ginger root and lemon sliced thin may
be used.


Tomato Manages.


Select round, smooth tomatoes for this
pickle. With a sharp knife cut slice
from the stem end large enough to allow
you to remove the seeds, taking care that
you do not break the outside of the tomato.
After all the seeds are taken out stand
each tomato with it's corresponding stem
piece in picking tub or large stone
crock Salt the inside of each tomato and
cover the whole with cold water. Let them
stand in the brine for twenty-four hours.
Drain and wash with fresh cold water;
stand the tomatoes with cut side down to
drain out all the water Prepare stufing
in following proportion of materials: Chop
a cabbage and six tomatoes (green) fine and
put each separately into brine for twenty
four hours, then drain thoroughly. Then
chop fine few small cucumbers and white
onions. Mix all together and add ground
ginger, mace, allspice, black pepper, CHINA
mon, cheap nasturtium seeds quarter of
cup of horseradish, half an ounce of mixed
whole mustard seed and quarter of a cup Of
salad oil. Bruise all the spices and mix
them with the oil, then with the other in
gradients Put teaspoonful of sugar and
two whole cloves in each tomato; then stuff
with the filling. Fit the pieces on each
mango and sew with a white thread or
fasten by wrapping a string around the
mango. Pack them in stone jars or large
mouthed glass jars and cover them with
hot cider vinegar sweetened with pound
or more of sugar to each gallon of vinegar,
according to taste. If a few bits of horse
radish root are placed on top of each jar
the mangoes will keep better.


Green Tomato Butter.


Select tomatoes that are full grown. but
quite green. Slice them thin. Make a
syrup in proportion of one pound of sugar
to two pounds of tomatoes. Boil down
slowly for four hours until the butter is
smooth and thick, stirring frequently to
prevent sticking. Flavor with lemon when
done.


Green Tomato Chowchow.


Chop fine one peck of green tomatoes,

one pint of sugar and a few pieces of
horseradish root. Boil for five minutes, add

LONDON, February 13.-The detailed ac-
counts which have just reached here OF
Lord kitcheners combined movement to
drive out the Beers from the enclosure OF
block house lines show that the conflict
was very picturesque and the most eXcltlne
incident of the whole campaign. Although
apparently surrounded by an impenetrable
ring of fire and steel the Beers dauntess
bravery and dashing charges ultimately re-
suited in the majority's escape from the
meshes of Lord Kitcheners close-draWn
net. The British commanders scheme was
the most extensive ever carried out during
the present war. 1t consisted of continu-
Gus line over fifty miles in length. Lord
Kitchener, who personally directed the
operations. was in close touch, day and
night, with every detail of the movements.


Beers Avoided the Railways.


The Beers, though hard pressed. shrank
from attempting to cross the railroad.
which was patrolled throughout the night
by armored trains, equipped with powerful
searchlights. The train lights We're sup
plemented by stationary search lights and
the specta cuar effect. as witnessed from
the trains. was most striking. BY the side
of the railroad were the dark forms OF
men lying in trenches. or standing. doing
sentry duty. The gloom of the moonless
night was internationally relieved by the
sweep of the search lights


The battle at Heilbron ragged from
o'clock Friday night until o'clock Satur
day morning. Throughout the five hours
fearful ring of fire from rifles. cannon and
pom-poms swept along the British lines. in
holding De Vets Beers. who made repeated
attempts to break out of the circle of
troops. From various positions, behind
rocks and dongas. the Beers kept up Wig
orous fusillade hoping to find weak spot
In the line. simultaneously others charged,
but again and again We're the Beers re-
pulsed. leaving dead. wounded and prison
ers in the hands of the British.


Beers Understood the Plan.


At the outset of the preparations the
Beers realized that the operations were not
merely an ordinary drive but a move
ment threatening them with total annihla-
ton, and General De Wet assembled his
whole force and discussed the situation
with the commanders, with the result that
the Beers were split up into three forces.
On Thursday night 800 Beers, headed by
Van Golfers, rushed a force of the imperial
Light Horse. yelling Storm, burghers.''
About 100 Beers got through, but the re-
mainder encountering tremendous fire.
We're turned back.


Friday nights conflict ebbed and swelled
over an area of forty to fifty miles, in which
the long hunted harassed and desperate
men endeavored to find outlets. The Beers,
at one spot. got within thirty yards Of the
British firing line. but the barbed wire
balked the burghers and forced them to re-
treat


The firing never ceased Aided by the
electric searchlights, the British narrowed
the surrounding territory with shrapnel,
shells and Maxim bullets. In the northern
section the Beers made desperate effort
to break through. Collecting q number Of
cattle. tie Beers drove them down on the
British lines. Bending low in their saddles,
the Beers rode among the cattle, making it
impossible to distinguish them In the dark
ness.


Pickets Opened Fire.


The British pickets opened terrible fire,
and the Beers were everywhere met with
relentless hail of bullets. A long line Of
flame ran up and down the firing line, near
ly thirty miles in length, as the armored
trains flashed their searchlights over miles
Of country. The reports Of the quick-firng
guns along the intrenched line and the
booming of the field guns and pom-poms
sounded very deep amid the sharp crack
ling Of the musketry, while Heilbrun Fort
contributed to the universal din with the
deep roar of it's naval gun.


This lasted for some twenty minutes,
when gre dually the rattle died down, until
only the crack of single shots was heard.
Then all was again quiet.


The Beers attempt to break the British
circle had failed. A few Of them succeed
ed in crossing the line, and among them
was Gen. De Wet.

Paterson, Feb 10 (SpeciaD.-The fable of the
phoenix is being rewritten here. Already the
shock of Sunday mornings disaster has passed.
and strangers coming within the gates OF TINS
industrial beehive are amazed at the equipose.
the cheerfulness and philosophical spirit of
the townspeople. Dependency and pessimlsm
are almost unknown qualities. Every one you
meet is more confident than another that the
city will quickly get on its feet again, bigger,
stronger and more ornate than ever


To-day business men and lawyers, bankers
and investors stood gazing at the ruins and dis
cussed plans for rebuilding. Men met each
other and smilingly swapped stories of personal
loss-books, records, papers-which could not be
replaced. Nobody was looking for sympathy,
and if there any who imagined that their
tale of woe overshadowed that of their fellows
the moral and mental atmosphere pervading the
town hushed them ere their dirge had yet
begun.


ute to the self-relance of people who were
now showing qualities of which they had hith-
erto deemed themselves incapable, and with
which no outsider had credited them. Pater-
sons repute If the truth must be told, had not
been quite so high as that OF some of its sister
cities. Many had regarded it as money grub
bing place, where the scramble for wealth had
developed abnormal selfshness and had dead
ened the moral and intellectual forces Of the
community. What will go down into history
as THE Great Fire has changed all that,


If the Inhabitants had studied moral phi





since childhood they could not we'll have come
out Of this ordeal better than they have during
the last forty-eight hours. Everybody seemed
anxious 10 know what he could do for his neigh
hor- Self-reliance evident everywhere.
and there were practically no appeals for aid
or charity of any kind.


Everywhere one observed good nature, even
optimism. and this applied well TO the tired
soldier. fireman ana policeman as TO the victims
who found themselves homeless or without
a shelter to conduct their business. There was
no lamentation-no weeping or Wallng ana no
growing. Each person was apparently Vying
with his neighbors in the matter of masking
misfortune with a smile and all were reader
talk about the future than to make
smoking debris and gable walls which stood as
eloquent monuments to structures which nut
yesterday had pleased the eye because of their
beauty. and respect because of their seeming
strength.


This fire of February @. 1902 will not hurt
Paterson. Undoubtedly il must take some In
dividuals years TO recover from the material
loss, especially few of the smaller ShOpkeepers
who had no insurance But the city itself Will
come out of it. five six years hence, better
than ever in every way. Meanwhile there may
be some temporary embarrassments and dlff-
culties but these Will not prove lnsuperable TO
the people who have shown such spirit as has
been manifested here and is being shown now.
The industries of the town are not affected.
Work is going on merrily in the mills and once
The rubbish is cleared away thousands of
nssons, carpenters and builders will swarm
around to cover the vacant spaces with sub
stantial and in some cases handsome buildings.


Morally and intellectually Paterson has met
with stoical fortitude the work of the Destroying
Ar gel. Ere many days the triumph of material
rehabilitation will have begun.

The fiords (fjords) of Scandinavia are ESQ

which you could see nothing till fairly in it.

siDpi or the st. Lawrence with its Thousand
Islands. But you are sailing the great Nor
wegian coast fiord-r river with it's more than
ten thousand islands. These islands are the
skrmish lines of the great mountains sent
down to protect the Norwegian shores against
the storms of the These fords were
the great naval academies of the old vikings
where they first learned the art of naviga-
lion and where they were trained from boy
hood to risk the perils of the waves and find
the coasts beyond. Wonders of the world
are the mountains, valleys rivers, fords,

Panama, Jan. 29.-The Colombian Government
fleet, consisting of the steamers Boyaca and
Chucuito. and the armed launch General Campo
which left here yesterday morning to make an
attempt to break the blockade of Aqua Duice
where the revolutionary fleet was last seen and
to communicate with General Castro the Co
lombian commander met the insurgent steamer
Padilla at Yeguala. thirty miles from Panama
at / o'clock yesterday afternoon, and opened
fire on her. The revolutionary steamers Daren
and Gaitan appeared on the scene soon after
the engagement began. The fire of the Chucuito
was so we'll directed that it caused the revolu-
tionary fleet to draw in toward the shore where
the enemy's ships were protected by land bat
teres. The Chucuto and the Boyaca then re-
tired unmolested. and arrived here at o'clock
yesterday evening. The General Campo was not
engaged.


The forces of General Herrera, the revolution
airy commander at San Carlos forty miles
from Panama.


Yeguala is the port of San Carlos.


The Boyaca will probably sail from Panama
again tonight.

lowing curved almost a circle. and the banks

LONDON, Jan. 1.-THE Pail Mall Ga
zette" has made an investigation into the
report that American silversmiths we're
preparing to invade the English market
with their goods.


Hitherto the trouble has been the dif-
ficulty of obtaining the hall mark (the
official stamp Of the goldsmith's company
and other assay Offices in the United
kingdom) after the goods had been fin
1shed. The report was that the Americans
had arranged to overcome this difficulty
by shipping partly finished goods and hav-
ing>them hall marked. Then they would
be returned and finished.


The Gazette" made investigations in
the chief silversmith sections OF Sheffield
and London and found that the method
is not new. France, Russia. Germany. and
Austria adopted it some years age.


Such goods bear the additional mark F.
which shows that they are of foreign
manufacture.


The "Gazette's" investigator concludes
that American competition need NOT be
feared, because the double freight would
wipe out the profit, and American makers
would be obliged to comply with English
standards of quality, which would mean
that they would have to raise their own.
He adds that American taste and ma
ch'ne workmanship in precious metals
nave never been popular in Great Britain

Through fog and mist. and over the soggy
turf of the Country Club near Brookline,

the best women golfers OF the country, In
a qualifying round Of the national cham-
pionship, and when the last player had COW
cred the three miles and had completed the
eighteen holes 1t was found that Miss Mar
garet Curtis of the Essex County Club,
Manchester, Mass, and Miss LouisaA Wells
Of the home club had excelled all others
and were tied for the first place with scores
Of 50 each. Following close at their heels
were Miss Ruth Underhill Of the Nassau
Country Club. Glen Cove, L. l.. and Miss
Georgianna Bishop Of the Brooklawn Golf
Club of Bridgeport. Conn. also tied for
third place with scores of 30 each. Miss
Curtis and Miss Wells and the winner OF
the tie between Miss Underhill and Miss
Bishop will receive Individual prizes given
by the association. Twenty-seven other
players, with scores ranging up to 1902. are
also in the running for the first round OF
match play today. Two more players. Mrs
]. T. Hubbard of the Harbor Hill Club.
Staten Island. and Mrs. Alex. McGregor Of
the Oakley Country Club. WATERFOWL
Mass, were tied for the thirty-second po-
stion. with scores Of 103


There were forty eight other players who
completed the course and handed in cards
with scores ranging from 1O4 to 133, but
they will have to wait until next year for
another chance at championship honors.
Nine players withdrew.


The low scoring, in spite Of the lifeless
turf and slow putting green, was sur
prise of the tournament. No less than
twenty-four players bettered 100, seven
were below 95, while the work of Miss Cur
tbs and Miss Wells in breaking 80 deserves
the highest praise. The play Of Miss Gene
We've Hecker, last years champion, and
Mrs. E. A. Manice, who defeated her in the
spring, was somewhat disappointing. Both
were erratic at the start and lost many
strokes in the outward journey, but. coming
back, each steadied perceptibly and finished
strong.


Considering the condition Of the turf.
which gave very little roll to the ball. the
driving was remarkable. Miss Curtis. Miss
Anthony. Miss Bishop, Miss Underhill and
Miss Adams repeatedly made ITO and $50
yards. while some drives reached over 200.
Some of the long iron work was also good,
but, as usual, in all women's events, the
putting was the feature. If the greens were
a trif1e slow. they were remarkably true,
and once the players got the roll OF the ball,
two. three and courtyard puts were COM
mon. Very few players took more than two
on any of the greens. and in this way made
up for many mistakes through the fair
green


The play was the best ever shown by wo-
men in championship event, the scores
being several strokes better than at Baltus-
rol last year. The dull weather kept down
the gallery. and the course was compare
lively clear all day. Miss Hecker's play
seemed to be the attraction, but after three
or four holes had been played the gallery
paid more attention to her partners Miss
Anthony. who played the first nine holes
Manice, while Miss Curtis and Miss Wells

The weather bureau has issued the fol-
lowing statement Of crop conditions for
November:


The month was marked by exceptionally
mild temperatures in all districts east of
the Rocky mountains. with excessively
heavy rains the north Pacific coast and
from the lower Missouri valley to the west
gulf coast. and more than the average
amount over large portion of the south
Atlantic and east gulf states


The reports generally show that winter
wheat was in very promising condition at
the close Of the month. With ample mois-
ture and exceptionally mild temperatures
throughout the month the crop made rapid
advancement and too rank growth is very
generally reported from the central valleys,
Oklahoma and Texas. In the early sown
the hessian fly has appeared extensively.
but this pest has not affected the late sown.
which constitutes much the greater part Of
the total acreage In Texas some fields OF
the early sown are from twelve to sixteen
inches high. and are liable to injury from
cold. On the north Pacific coast the weather
has been very unfavorable for seeding.

NEW YORK. March 2O.-The main
tendency of the stock market today, dur
ing the greater part of the session. was
toward further price improvement and in
scme quarters there were exhibitions of
decided strength. Many of the most pro-
nounced fluctuations. however, were in
comparatively unimportant stocks of the
class designated spccialties. In that
quarter considerable activity prevailed.
and as rule it was difficult TO account
for the movements other than that they
resulted from more or less skillful manip-
ulation.


Quick Profits Reaped.


1t frequently happened that a group of
market operators would take up partic-
ular stock. move it up sharply and depend
upon outside traders to buy their pur-
chases, when. after reaping quick profit,
they would transfer their work to some
other stock that could be easily manipu-
lated.


News bearing on the market was meagre
in the extreme Weather reports, as far
as they related to the crop situation.
were favorable and Western advices said
that the outlook in that direction was
quite as hopeful as could be expected.
Nothing very definite was received from
the miners convention now in progress in
Shamokin. but an early despatch said that
the delegates who are opposed to a strike
have a controlling majority of thirty-six,
xvb fla 2 ba Loo oF fba ad Work
ers' Union was quoted as counseling cau-
tion. The iron and steel industry furnish
ed reports of increasing business with the
outlook decidedly satisfactory.


London Market Heavy.


Foreign exchange markets were dull
and steady, with the enquiry for bills held
in check by the absence of fast steamers
sailing for Europe this week. The tone
of the London market was heavy and this
tone was ascribed to the check received
from the Kaffir boom. The Bank Of Eng
lands rate of discount remained unchang
ed at per cent. and the weeks returns
of that institution did not exhibit very
important changes.


There was an irregular opening, but the
market soon hardened and developed some
new features of speculative interest. The
improvement in the grangers extended to
the Pacific stocks, notably the St. Louis
and San Francisco issues. The anthracite
shares were slightly lower on feeling
of apprehension among room traders re-
garding the labor situation.


fractions Quiet, but Firm.

Of uncertainty gave way TO one of moder-
ate strength. Relatively little trading
took place in the members of the traction

The litigation instituted against the pro-

seriously. Traders, however, were dis

politan and Brooklyn Rapid Transit stock

Colorado Fuel and Iron, General Elec-

Pretoria, dated today. Lord Kitchener
sends details Of the disaster to the escort
Of the convoy of empty wagons at Vondo-
mop. southwest Of Klerksdorp. Transvaal
colony. The British casualties in killed,
wounded and men made prisoners reach
the total OF 632. In addition, the Beers
captured two guns. Lieut.. Col. Anderson
who commanded the British force and who
has returned to kraaipan, Cape Colony
with nine officers and 245 men, reports that
when his advanced guard was within ten
miles of Klerksdorp. during the morning
of February 25, the Beers opened heavy
rifle fire on the troops from the scrub The
burghers were driven off and the convoy
resumed its march. when a more deter
mined attack was made on the cOnvoy's
left flank, the Beers getting within a hun
dred yards and stampeding the mules har-
messed to a number Of wagons The at
tacking forces were again driven off, At
about 6:3O o'clock in the morning the rear
guard was attacked by a strong force of
Beers. and simultaneously another body of
Beers charged the center Of the convoy
and stampeded the mules in all directions
throwing the escort into confusion, during
which the Beers charged ana recharged
riding down the separated British units The
fighting lasted for two hours, during which
the two British gums and pom-pom al
most exhausted their ammunition. de-
tachment of 200 mounted infantry from
Klerksdorp attempted to reinforce the
Beers.
Lieut.. Col. Anderson adds that the
strength OF the Beers was estimated at
Kemps. Ceiiiers. Lemmer. Wolmarans and
Potgieter were all present. Commandant
Lemmer IL said to have been killed.

A dispatch from Pekin yesterday says:
All evidences indicate that the Emperor
of China is now more completely under
the domination of the dowager empress
than he was before the Chinese court went
into exile. Several high officials were
granted audiences today, during which the
emperor filled the role of figurehead. The
dowager empress sat on his majesty's left
and conducted the conversations. Accord
ing to the accounts of two of the officials
who were received today, the dowager en-
press ignored the emperor. and the latter
did not attempt to take any part in the
affair. These officials say his majesty ap-
peared melancholy and listless.


The principal topic of conversation dur
ing these audiences was the presence in
Pek1n of the foreign garrisons. The
dowager empress seemed impressed with
the necessity of a conciliatory policy.


Evidence accumulates pointing to the
timidity of the dowager empress about
coming back to Pekin. Her first remark X
upon alfghting at the Machiapu station
yesterday was, Where are the foreign
soidlers! Upon seeing number of news
paper correspondents at the station the
dowager empress bowed to them obseaui-
ously. Before leaving Pao-Ting-Fu in the
special train yesterday the dowager .em-
press requested Traffic Manager Foley Of
the railroad not to use the locomotive wflis-
tie, explaining that she was extremely
nervous, and that the whistle frightened
her

rate the American and Japanese officers
VINO guarded the imperial palace during
the courts absence. She will also confer
decorations upon the officers and engf-
neers who had charge of the imperial
train during the railroad journey from
Pao-Ting- Flu.

A dispatch from New York yesterday
says: In broad daylight a collision which
might have resulted in dreadful calamity
occurred in New York harbor this afternoon
between an incoming passenger liner and an
outbound freight steamer.


The steamship Liguria Of the Italian Roy
al Mail Steamship Company, with over 100
persons on board, was run down in the Mar
rows by the British steamer Peconio of the
Mediterranean and New York Steamship
Company. bound out for ports in the Medi-
terranean. A succession of whistle blasts.
just how blown could not be learned, was
followed by a tremendous crash and the
Peconic's bow smashed into the hull of the
Lguria just forward of the foremast


The Italian liners hull was cut to the
waters edge and water poured into the
aperature The Peconic, as she drifted
away, scraped the white hull of the Liguria
and carried away the companion ladder.
The bow Of the Peconic on the port side
was stove in and the stem turned to star
board


On board the liner all was confusion for
few minutes. but Capt. Montana restored
order promptly and forced the steerage pas
sengers over to the starboard side In order
to bring the hole cut by the Peconic above
the water. This effort was so successful
that very little water entered the liner.


The pilot who brought the Liguria into
port Frank Kramer. was little disposed to-
talk, but said the fault was all with the
Peconic. He said the Liguria was coming
along slowly toward the Narrows. The Pc
comic and the British steamer Antilia, bound
out for Nassau, were steaming to sea a
short distance apart when the Peconic blew
two whistles and then changed the signals
The Liguria sheered to starboard and then
back at full speed. The impact came with
terrific force, the sound being heard on the
shore.


The Peconic was so damaged that she re-

initial run yesterday since the arrival of

Vernon. She went over the course several

Fergus Falls, Mimi, April 24.-Tues-
days rain and snow storm were just what
was needed in this section Of the state.
The seeding is practically finished and
the ground was becoming altogether too
dry, grain that had been in for ten days
not having sprouted. Warm weather will
bring both grass and grain forward at a
rapid rate, as the ground has been thor
oughly soaked.


Hallock, Mimi, April 24.-Wheat seed
ing In Kittson county is fully one-half
over. The weather has been perfect,
cloudy and somewhat cool and the soil
never In better condition to receive the
grain. A great many of the smaller farm
ers are through and now seeding other
grains. The acreage will be about the
same as last year. The fax average will
be increased somewhat.

French red tape in all its beauty.

Peking. Feb. 1.-The Empress Dowager, the
Emperor and the Empress this afternoon re-
ceived the women and children of the members
OF the diplomatic corps in the private apart
ments Of the palace. The audience was the
most revolutionary affair since the return of
the court to Peking. The exclusiveness of Chi
nese royalty and the prejudices against the
meeting of the sexes was waived and the func-
ton was less formal than is usual in European
courts. The Empress Dowager occupied the
throne. with brilliant assemblage Of princesses
and court women about her. The Emperor was
seated upon a small platform in the centre of
the room.


The visitors upon entering bowed twice to the
Emperor. and several of them ascended the
throne and bowed to the Empress Dowager
Mrs. Conger, wife Of United States Minister
Conger, as doyeness of the diplomatic corps
read speech, which was translated by Secre-
tary Williams Mrs. Conger said


We heartily congratulate you and the i'm
perial court that the unfortunate situation
which led you to abandon your beautiful capital
has been so happily resolved that you are now
permitted to return in freedom and peace The
events OF the last two years must have been as
painful to you to the rest of the world. but
the sting of the experience may be eliminated
by the establishment OF franker more trustful
and friendler relations between the Chinese
and the other peoples of the earth. The world
-
be stayed, and 1T Is hoped that China will join
with the great sisterhood of nations in the
grand march The recent imperial edicts give
promise of great good to your people and to
your vast empire


The Dowager's reply was exceedingly friendly
in tone. 1t was in part follows:


Last year the dissensons in the palace caused
a revolution which compelled our hasty depart
ure. but it is a great qualification to us that
Capital caused such
in China and abroad.


Baron Czikann. the Austrian Minister and
doyen Of the Diplomatic Corps presented all the
women TO the Empress Dowager, who took the
hand of each OF them. They were next present
ed to the Emperor. who also shook hands with
them. The guests then retired to ante-ro6m
The Empress Dowager. entering this room
grasped Mrs. Conger's hand, which she held for
.Cme minutes. trembling, wAering and sobbng
loudly and exclaiming in broken sentences that
the attack upon the legations was terrible mis-
take and that she repented it bitterly. In re-
ply. Mrs Conger assured her that the past
would be forgotten Bracelets and rings Of
great value were then placed upon Mrs. Conger's
wrists and fingers. The Empress Dowager made
INQUIRIES regarding the other women who were
in Pekng during the siege of the legations. and
Mines Rainbridge and Morisse, the wives of
Secretaries Bainbridge and Morsse, of the

ed and warmly greeted.

This was spread upon three tables. the En-

A dispatch from Madrid yesterday says:
The brilliant weather today encouraged the
crowds to pour out into the streets OF the
city. and every thoroughfare was filled with
merrymakers.


The appearance of the streets was in
strong contrast to the scene which at the
same time was being enacted within the
palace. Here the festivity gave place to a
drama. The queen regent of Span was
sorrowfully taking leave of her ministers
and practically relinquishing to her son the
solemn charge which she has so faithfully
fulfilled for the past sixteen and a half
years.


Premier Sagasta and his colleagues pro-
ceeded to the palace at IL o'clock this morn
ing for formal leave-taking of the queen
regent, and to present for her maiesty's
signature the last DEGREES to which her
hand and seal will ever be affixed as regent
of Spain.


When the queen regent withdrew her pen
from the parchment comforting the Order of
the Golden Fleece upon the Duke of Cum
berland her eyes were moist. Her regency
really terminated at this time. although
until the king takes the oath in the presence
of the chambers, May IL, his mother re-
mains officially the queen regent.


1t was a pathetic scene when the minis
tiers We're ushered into the queen regents
cabinet. She received them with the young
king at her side. Premier Sagasta, in an



in behalf of himself and his colleagues. re-
called the day when the queen regent, fresh
from the grief Of her widowhood, honored
him with her confidence, although she
scarcely knew him. He compared that day
to this. when the young king, with his de-
voted mother at his side, was about to enter
upon an exercise of his constitutional pre-
rogative.


new reign would be pregnant with greater
achievements and greater blessings to the
nation than the preceding reign had been.


The queen regent listened to Senior Sa-
gasta with increasing emotion. Finally,
with tears running down her cheeks, she
responded and thanked him. Her majesty
said however short of her own ideal she
might have fallen, she always had the well
fare of the country sincerely at heart, and
had done what she could to repay the loving
Kindness always shown her. She said she
hoped the councillors would help her son
as they had helped her, because, although
the king might possess natural gifts, he
was still young and needed the help of good
advice.


Then, after signing the decree fixing the
ceremonial of taking the oath for May
H. the queen regent announced her desire
to modify this ceremonial. Her majesty
said that on May II her governmental func-
tons would cease, and she would then be-
come simply the queen dowager, jealous
for the welfare of her children, but stand
ing absolutely aside from public affairs.
Therefore, her majesty explained that she
desired to go to the chamber accompanied
solely by her daughters, as the widow of
the late monarch, without any ostentation.
and receiving only the honors due her per-
sonal rank.


Premier Sagasta respectfully replied that
the ministers were unable to accede to her
majesty's desire in this matter, because,
until the king took the oath, she was still
the regent and ought to accompany her son
until the last solemn moment. The queen
regent yielded to Premier Sagasta's repre-
sensations and agreed to accompany the
king to the steps of the throne.

Miss Dorothy Stiles, daughter of William
Stiles, aretired chemist, formerly of Columbus,
Ohio, is dying at her fathers home, seven
miles south of Bay City, Mich, with disease
that has baffled every physician called in to
attend her. She is 16 years old, and until
few months ago was in perfect health. Her
body seems slowly turning into marble, or q
substance resembling it.


One night, while bathing, the girl found that
her heels were perfectly white and hard like
stone. She called her mothers attention to
the fact, and Mrs. Stiles was terrified on ex-
amining the girls body. She found that both
heels, the tips of her shoulder blades and her
hips were similarly affected The condition
has spread until now both legs above the ankles
have become stony. The hips of the afflicted
girl have no longer the power to bend and the
power of action has been taken from her
shoulders. She says she suffers no pain.


The doctors say that death must ensue with
in few months. They scout the theory re-
garding the case put forth by the girls almost
demented father. He says he was experiment.
ing with some drugs in the bathroom, used
the bathtub for the purpose and neglected to
cleanse it. The same night his daughter took
a bath in this tub, and the father insists that
the chemicals have produced the terrible dis
ease. The girl takes no nourishment but
liquids, and those with difficulty.

Special Dispatch TO The Evening Star.


NEW YORK. June e.-opsning prices this
morning were generally steady around last
weeks closing level. but later trading dis
closed hardening tendency under limited
dealings. London was dull and unintercst-
ing and local commission business was re-
stricted. Traders were inclined TO cover
short stock result Of the decline In
wheat and the generally favorable crop
news.


Toward the end of the first hour the mar
ket rallied nearly l per cent and there was
some slight Improvement in the character
Of the demand. An effort To get the mar
ket out of It's rut was in evidence hut
prices responded more easily Than the vol
ume OF business, the advances mp TO noon
having been recorded on transactions aEgre-
eating only 1o3.0DO shares


During the early afternoon dullness was
pronounced, hut prices held well In snita NJ
the lack of business


The railroad list was strong In tone large
~ because the routine news was favorable
mon Pacific was firm within narrow
limits. but St Paul showed the effects of
short covering and responded more substau-
TALLY. Missouri Pacific was In fair demand.
shade under par, and stress was again
ialu upon the improving outlook FOR a closer
union If the Gould properties.


Here and there throughout the list there
were suggestions of revival of old enter
prises in connection with the more eco
HpiHlG management OF railway nrNnPTtiFS
Part of this effort was undoubtedly in
tended to distract attention from the one
decided handicap TO Improvement. namely.
the coal strike


News from the coal region was construed
to be more favorable. but for no reason
other than that the operators were said To
be holding their own. The strike In the
soft coal fields was not factor in the mar
ket, the movement in that section not be-
ing considered wholly successful.


Reading was advanced 1 per cent under
buying by interests supposed TO be accu-
mulating the stocks for purposes entirely
removed from the present labor difficulty
The strength of this property seemed to
hold the entire list OF coal stocks steady at
fractional gains.


Hearings upon the subject of the iniunc-
tion asked for to restrain the United States
Steel Company from converting it's pre-
fcrred stock into bonds have been set for
tomorrow. This action is regarded as an
expression of hostility TO the corporation
and is intended to embarrass the manage
ment rather than to ward off any personal
loss.


Because of this view the street paid little
attention to the matter. the steel stocks
merely fuctuating with the general market.


In the industrial list the movement OF
prices was irregular under very limited
dealings. Good buying of National Lead
was reported, and there was fair demand
for American Sugar and the Fuller Cor
struction Company's stock.


Money was in fair supply and there was
no indication Of any significant change in
interest rates. Safety along this line, how
ever. hinges very largely upon a decreased
speculative demand. The banks are not in
position to foster market activity and to
meet the seasons demands from other
sources. Public interest can scarcely be
al oused until after the crops are assured
and this prospect will leave the market
under the control of the professional trader
for the full midsummer season.


During the last hour prices held well

Washington's base ball fans received
good news from Chicago last night when
the report came in that the Senators had
defeated the champion white sox by the
score of 4 to l. Victories have been few
and far between for the eastern teams on
this western trip, and now the Senators
are up with the bunch. Boston has won
only three games. the Athletics two and
Baltimore ore. Yesterdays victory makes
the second for Washington. Incidentally,
the Senators resumed their rightful posi-
tion at the head of the second column, once
more showing Cleveland to the rear. as rain
prevented the game between the Spiders
and the Athletics


Albert Orth got back into his normal
form, and as result the Chicago cham
pions had to be content with five hits dur
Ing the nine innings. OF this number
Mertes secured a double and a single, and
the other three bingles were distributed
between Strang, Isbell and Daily. In only
one inning, the seventh, were the white Sox
able to get together more than one hit. and
the bngles by Mertes and Daily scored
Chicago's solitary run.


Back of Orth, the Senators fielded nicely,
two misplays. fumbles by Lee and Ely, be-
ing the only errors charged against
them. Neither one was costly. Careys
game of Wednesday brought out renewed
weakness in his injured wrist, and he had
to remain on the bench yesterday, Dele
nanty going to first and Lee into left field.
"Old Reliable Ely was back in the game
after a days rest. and his fielding and bat
ting was the feature of the game, although
CoughlinS work ran him close second.
The chances accepted by Ely were more
difficult, and for this reason he is given the
prestige over the Scranton boy.


Virgil Garvin did the twirling for Chi
cago, and although his work was good, in
comparison with Orth's it looked poor. But
eight hits were made by Washington, but
four different times the Senators got
couple of them together and runs re-
suited. Only one error was made back of
Garvin, a wild throw by Strang, but it was
of the disastrous sort, and led to the Sena-
tors getting their first two runs.


Washington's Good Start.


Both teams were blanked in the initial
inning, but in the second Washington Sc
cured a good start by scoring two runs.
Scranton BIZ Coughlin began business
with hot single to left. Lee tried to sac
rifce, sending a roller to Strang, at third,
and the Iatter's throw was wild enough
to pull Davis off second base and both
runners were safe. Ely tried to pull off an
other sacrifice, but instead looped a little
fly to Isbell and was out Coughlin got
tired waiting for base hits and bolted for
third like ten-second sprinter and by
splendid slide was safe. Seeing Coughlin's s



the throw down, which was little high to
DAILY, the Scranton boy dashed for home
and made the plate by regular Doylesque
slide. Lee was now on second, but Clarke
struck out and another run looked away
on Mr. Orth then ambled to the plate and
coolly plunked out a screeching single over
second base, the fleet footed Lee racing
home.


In the fifth the Senators hung up an
other tally, blanks being served out to the
champions In the meantime. Ryan was
the leader-off this time with nice single
and Doyle pushed him along with a sac
rifce. A passed ball allowed Ryan to scoot
to third and 'Del's' long fly to center
field enabled him to score.


In the seventh Chicago broke the ice
and scored its solitary run. With one out
Mertes singled over second and moved up
base while Isbell was being thrown out
at first by Coughlin. Tom Daily followed
with timely single into left and Mertes
raced home.


In the ninth Washington scored its
fourth and last run. CoughIin was passed

supposed to explain the unusual record.

pneumonia in February, and the average
for March is not more than half the fig

than usual. There were eight deaths,
against two for February. The breaking
up OF the river and the consequent de-
terloration OF the water supply is the
chief cause ascribed.

iberia and two from scarlet fever.

Madrid, May 1.-THE brilliant weather to-
ssy encouraged the crowds to pour out into the
streets Of the city and every thoroughfare was
sIIed with merrymakers who were apparently
IN the happiest humor.


The appearance of the streets was In strong
contrast TO the scene which at the same time
was being enacted within the palace. Here the
festivity gave place to a drama. The Queen
Regent OF Spain sorrowfully taking leave OF
her ministers and practically relinquishing 10
the hands of her son the solemn charge which
she has so faithfully fulfilled for the last sixteen
and a half years.


Premier Sagasta and his colleagues proceeded
10 the palace at IL o'clock this morning for a
formal leave taking Of the Queen Regent and to
present for her majesty's signature the last
DEGREES to which her hand and seal will ever be
affixed as Regent of Spain.


When the Queen Regent withdrew her pen
from the parchment conferring the order of the
Golden Fleece upon the Duke Of Cumberland
her majestys eyes were moist. Her regency
really terminated at this time although until
the King takes the oath in the presence OF the
combined Chambers May II his mother
mains officially the Queen Regent.


It was a pathetic scene when the ministers
we're ushered into the Queen Regents cabinet
She received them with the young King at her
side. Premier Sagasta. in an eloquent address,
delivered in behalf OF himself and his colleagues.
recalled the day when the Queen Regent. fresh
from the grief Of widowhood. honored him with
her confidence. although she scarcely knew him.
He compared that day TO this when the young
King with his devoted mother at his side. was
about to exercise his constitutional prerogative.
81 was Prime Minister then. and am Prime
Minister now" said Sehor Sagasta. In the in
tervening years the speaker said. the noble
Queen Regent had been a slave to duty. She
had sacrificed her youth to the jealous guardian
ship Of her children. She had suffered much,
but found compensation to-day in the happiness
Of the King.


Turning the King, Senor Sagasta compared
the difficulties which confronted him to-day
with the situation at the death Of the late King,
his father. The present difficulties" said the
Premier, "are not insurnountable. Spain has
not progressed as much might be desired;
still, she has made substantial progress. Peace
and tranquility have been secured. the of
military pronunclamentos is past, and the atten-
ton of the people is centred in education and
labor"


Premier Sagasta said also that he hoped the
new reign would be pregnant with greater
achievements and greater blessings to the ma
tion than the preceding reign had been.


The Queen Regent listened 10 Sehor Sagasta
with increasing emotion. Finally, tears run
ming down her cheeks. she responded and
thanked the Premier for his words. Her
majesty said that, however short she might
have fallen from her own ideal, she had always
had the welfare Of the country sincerely at
heart and had done what she could TO repay
the loving kindness which had always been
shown to her. She said she hoped the coua-
cillors before her would help her son IS they
had helped her, because. although the Kins
might possess natural gifts, he was still young
and needed good advice


Then, after signing the decree fixing the cere-
rnonial Of taking the oath for May II, the Queen
Regent announced her desire to modify this
ceremonial Her majesty said that on May IL
her governmental functions would cease. and
that she would then become simply the Queen
dren but standing absolutely aside from public
affairs. Therefore. her majesty explained. she
desired to go 10 the Chamber accompanied solely
BY her daughters as the widow OF the late
monarch without any Gstentation and receiving
only the honors due her personal rank.


Premier Sagasta respectfully replied that the
ministers were unable TO accede to her mai
estv's desires in this matter because until the
King took the oath she was still the Regent
and ought to accompany her son until the last
solemn moment.


The Queen Regent yielded to Premier Sa-
gasta's representations and agreed TO accom-
pany the King 10 the steps of the throne.

NEW YORK, October 24.-Prices were
generally steady in today's stock market
and routine developments were mainly of
an encouraging nature. London was dull
and irregular and suggested no significant
action in the local market. Traders hes
tated to sell under the circumstances and
the larger interests showed little DISPOSE
ton to buy.


Dizziness was the most conspicuous fea-
ture of the days business, and bankers
generally regarded that tendency the
most natural and the most desirable.


Colorado Fuel and Iron was advanced
about per cent under buying for purposes
of control The fact that the leaders of
both factions are in this city gave some
color to the theory that the purchases were
for voting purposes at the December meet
ing. The reaffirming of the report that the
railroad interests represented by the Gould
and Hawley holdings were taking a more
conspicuous place in the contest helped to
advance the price. The convertible bonds
Of the company were active and higher for
similar reasons.


American Cotton Oil common was bought
on the prospect of a substantial increase in
dividend, probably to per cent. The In
dustriat list was favored in what little
new buying there was. The Steel stocks
were steady, and the miscellaneous low
priced shares reflected fair demand.


In the railroad list Missouri Pacific was
given good support, and there was a list
less demand for Union Pacific around los
Canadian Pacific held well, and St. Paul
was cratic.


At one time an effort was made to adj
vance Baltimore and Ohio on the short
interest, but there was only moderate
rally. Norfolk and Western was taken
around II, but 1t failed to advance ma
terially.


The entire list moved but slightly and
good news was absolutely lacking In the
requirements for rallying prices.
The money situation for the day was the
most satisfactory since the stringency be-
gan. Two Of the larger banks loaned over
coded from to 3 per cent for loans carry
ing over until Monday and time money IN
der the legal rate appeared in some volume.
Sterling exchange was easier, posted
rates declining y per cent. and gold ship
ments are put further off in consequence.
The banks have gained from the subtreaS-
ury during the week $40. 800. 600 and have
lost but trif1e over 81 600 900 to the in
terror. The bank statement tomorrow
should be favorable in consequence of this
showing, and today's large loans will not
appear.


For some reason traders sought to make
no capital out Of this prospect, and the va
riOus pools were credited with a desire 10

early next week. There are many plans

London, Feb. 5.-The English Zion
lists held a great meeting at the
Shoreditch town hall. Israel Zangwell,
the novelist, made an eloquent speech.
He strongly attacked the administration
of the millions bequeathed by the late
Baron Hirsch, which bequest, he declared,
was being rendered useless by the Jewish
colonization society's simply throwing
good money after bad. It's projects, he
added, were few and unfit.


The Jews could not wait much longer
for Palestine. The world was waking up
and the concession they wanted might be
granted to others, and the wandering Jew
would find himself turned from his own
door. The road to Palestine could be
paved only with gold. Baron Hirsch' S
millions must come to Zionism. The
money, however, would be useless with
out the physical and moral regeneration
of the Jewish people. Money, muscle and
morals were the three things on which
Zionism was to be built. There were far
too many money lenders, bankruDts and
bloodsucking landlords among them. Mr..
Zangwill was given a great ovation.

Holland owes much Of its unique charm
and the Dutch race many of it's distinc-
tive qualities to the gaily painted and hap
PLY peopled homes that float sereneIy
through the landscapes of the Netherlands.
Nearly every Dutch "tjalk' or barge is not
only a conveyance for merchandise but

temporary habitation as a sea-going ship

home. The raised poop, upon which the
owner stands grasping the tiller and watch
ing the sail directing the labors Of his
family at the tow rope, is the roof of the
house. 1t is also the garden by virtue OF
its row of pots containing Towering plants
and bulbs. Here, when the days voyage is
ended, and the house moored for the night,
the good man smokes his biggest pipe and
drinks his schnapps; the women sit and
sew; the children safely inclosed by the
poop rail and a little toy gate, play their
stolid games. and the canary and the Sis
kin from their gilded cages pour forth
rival evensongs.

The cable match between the Americans
and the English for the Newnes cup ended,
after two days hard fight, last Saturday eve
ming, with a victory Of 5A to Az in favor Of
the Americans. This is the seventh cable
match between the London and Brooklyn
Chess Clubs and the fourth victory for the
Americans. Last years match was a draw
Those of 1899 and 1900 were American victo-
ries, and those of 1897 and 1893 We're English
wins; the first match, that Of 1896, going to
the Americans. Three successive victories
are required to secure permanent possession
of the Newnes cup. Accordingly, last years
draw spoiled the American record of two
straight victories and compelled them to be-
gin anew in 1902. Special efforts doubtless,
will be made to repeat this months achieve
ment in 1903 and 1904.


This years American team was the same
as that Of 1901 with the exception that Del
mar replaced ShoWalter and Helms was sub
stituted for Bampton. In the British team,
Lawrence, Blake. Trenchard and Girdlestone
were substituted for Blackburne Ward, Jack
son and Jacobs. Napier, who, with Pillsbury
and Marshall, represented the United States
in the international tournament at Monte
don headquarters. Pillsbury and Marshall
crossed the channel the night before the
match and played their games over the open
boards. The fact that they did not meet ex-
pectations in their games-Pillsbury getting
only draw and Marshall losing his game
was probably due to loss OF sleep from the
stormy passage, neither Of them getting an
hours rest. Great interest centered in the
two games at the London club over the open
boards, even United States Ambassador Choate
honoring the event with his presence.

There are at present two brands of anti
imperialists, if such designation is not too
commercial in tone to apply to gentlemen
who insist that commercialism is now the
national sin.


Brand number one is represented by men
like Edward Atkinson. who have never for
a day approved of our course in the Phil
ippines. They have insisted from the very
outset that we were wrong in our first step.
Their pet phrase has always been that
Dewey should have sailed away promptly
after sinking the Spanish fleet In Manila
bay. Their position therefore has been per-
fectly consistent. However radically one
may differ with them. one must concede
consistency. and hear them with a sort of
patience and politeness when they descant
upon our difficulties in the archipelago.
They are thoroughly we'll convinced that
they were the wise men of that day. and
they remind US with sigh and a slow
shaking of the head that had their advice
been taken the country must have ESCAPED
its sorest troubles.


Brand number two is composed of men
like Senators Teller and Patterson and
Henry Watterson, who were imperialists to
the core at the time the flag was hoisted at
Manila, and for some time after. They
talked about destiny, about obligations to
humanity, about national pride, and about
the tenacity of the AnglO-SaXon race. They
were as certain as men could be that we
had done the proper thing in taking over
the archipelago, and they had only the Sc
verest structures for those who were hold
ing lack and proposing scuttle. The flag
will remain said Mr.. Teller. I'VE will
never retire. declared Mr. Pattersons Den
yer newspaper. I'VE will be there a hun
dred years from now" exclaimed Mr.. Wat
terson with characteristic confidence, "un-
less "A stronger power turns up meanwhile
and drives us OUT These men, and many
like them who are now clamoring for scut-
tie, supported the policy of Mr.. Mckinley
with the utmost loyalty.


What has since come over the spirit Of
their dream? What has converted them
into scuttlers more aggressive even than
the original scuttlers? What explains the
fact that they are now in the lead, with
the Atknsonians merely followers? Politics?
Are they willing to reverse themselves on
the subject OF destiny, the tenacity of the
Anglo-Saxon race, and all that. for mere
temporary partisan purposes? Are they
willing to trade the Philippine Islands for
control Of the next House Of Representa-
tives? Are they scuttlers for votes only.
with the secret conviction that in the end
scuttle a policy will be impossible of ex-
ecution?

The anthracite coal area is 483
square miles. Upon this territory
about 400, 900 persons are directly de-
pendent upon the mining industry for
their subsistence another 200, 900
are indirectly dependent upon it and
were necessarily affected by the recent
strike. Among this group pof 600, 900
souls industrial war prevailed for
nearly six months. The wages of
14o, 900 mine employees, which ag-
gregated monthly average of over
three and half millions of dollars,
were Immediately cut off. The whole
sale houses heard the sound of battle
from afar, and in the spring restrain
ed the activity of their agents and
watched developments. Conserva-
tive business men who saved from
five to ten per cent. on their purchases
by buying early in the season with
held their orders. The hotels where
commercial travellers stayed lost fifty
per cent. of their transient trade.
The banks found considerable fall
ing off in the deposits. Over the
hardware, clothing, jewelry, furni
ture, and dry-goods stores hung
depressing sense of impending calam-
ity. Before hostilities were declared
an ominous depression in business
circles throughout the anthracite coal
fields prevailed. May II proved how
we'll these men had read the signs of
the times. An army of 14o, 900 pro-
ducers did not respond that morning
to the gongs which sounded at the
four hundred colleries. The strug-
gle was on, and those men who had
watched the development of affairs
since 1900 felt in their hearts that it
was to be costly stubborn, and pro-
tracted one.


Society in the strike territory was
divided into two hostile camps, and
the line of cleavage was along the
antagonistic interests of capital and
labor. Mine superintendent, fore
men, clerks, and some favorite miners
in all about FIVE thousand strong
were on the side of the operators.
The rank and file of mine employees
were on the other side. The mer-
chants, from business considerations,
held their peace. Professional men
of influence were discreet, but their
conservatism and pecuniary interests
inclined them to the side of the oper-
ators more than to that of the men.
The clergy, cautious and timid, could
not prevent the spirit of faction from
entering the churches. A few were
outspoken, but the rank and file of
our spiritual leaders were silent and
prayed for peace.


Soon after the strike was declared
family and social bonds were severed.
For the first month mine workers
migrated in large numbers from all
anthracite communities. We had
over thirty thousand young Slav
bachelors in our towns and villages.
Hundreds of these packed their
trunks, carried them to the depot,
and left for either fatherland or else
where in quest of work. If any one
imagines that the Slavs are not sus-
ceptible to the ties of sympathy and
fellowship, he should have seen these
people at the depots They kissed
each other farewell, the departing
fingered on the platform of the train
and waved goodbye, and strong men
turned their faces to brush off the fall
ing tear. Some left stealthily. They
owed bill and feared attachment.
There were men at the depot watch
ing the migrating ones. The tax
collector was there. Merchants who
had information and their creditors
were leaving had constables attach
the goods in the depot. l saw one of
these debtors brought before justice
of the peace. The man was passive,
but the wife argued her case with
such effect that two dollars were taken
off the costs. The bill was paid, and
as the woman left, the constable said,
"She's a holy terror" The only
persons kept busy for the first month
of the strike were ticket agents, con-
stables, and justices of the peace.
One of this last class said in June,
Business is good I've taken in
over five dollars day for the last
month"


The English-speaking mine em-
ployees did not leave in troops, as did
the Slavs. Many families of them,
however, have left these coal fields.
In the towns of Mahanoy City and
Shenandoah houses were very scarce
before the strike; today the card
For rent" is seen in every street.
Few are the English-speaking fami-
lies throughout the anthracite regions
which have not been broken up.
! Young men and women were quick
to see the economic pressure which
soon would fall upon the family, and,
to stay it as long as possible, they took
their departure to the cities of New
York and Philadelphia, or to the soft
coal fields. The boys made many
heroic sacrifices. Money was scarce.
They would board freight train and
take Johnny Mitchell excursion
to some distant point. The cities OF
Easton, Allentown, New York, Phil
adelphia, etc., were soon glutted with
cheap labor. The boys begged their
food and tramped in quest of work.

Where tall pines crown the lonely hill
The unkempt grasses wave,
And shifting shadows ever weave


The semblance of a grave
From the long shade the passer-by


At MONDAY turns aside:
IT'S but a shadow on the path


Thy steed and thee may ride.
The stranger turns at dusk to catch


The white CLEAN of a stone;
Fear not for thou, save thy good steed,
Cross Quaker hill alone.
For voices with the wind shall speak,


Forms with the dusk uprise;
And swaying gallows creak, and steps


Be heard, and phantom cries.
The tall pines moan, the branches shake,
Slow falls the snow, and still:
The moaning night wind signs "Alas!"


Like the dead on Quaker hill.

Sweet little maid with winsome eyes
That laugh all day through the tangled hair.
Gazing with baby looks wise


Over the arm of the oaken chair
Dearer than you is none to me,


Dearer than YOU there be none
Since in your laughing face see


Eyes that tell of another one.
Here where the freight softly gows,


Sheltered and safe and snug and warm,
What to You is the wind that blows,


Driving the sleet of the winter storm7
Round your head the ruddy light


Glints the gold from your tresses spun
But deep is the drifting snow tonight,


Over the head of the other one.
Hold me close you sagely stand


Watching the dying embers shine;
Then shall / feel another hand


That nestled once in this hand of mine;
Poor little hand, so cold and chill,


Shut from the light of stars and sun,
Clasping the withered roses still


That hide the face of the sleeping one
Laugh. little maid, while laugh you may,
Sorrow comes TO us all, / know;
Better perhaps for her TO stay


Under the drifting robe of snow
Sing while you may your baby songs,
Sing till your baby days are done
But. OH the ache of the heart that longs
Night and day for the other one!

marked progress in remedying the OBJ
jectionable political and social condi-

tory for many years.

feverish, congested condition of the
country which prevailed short time

All day long crowds stared at the portraits

each a big wife and large family while,
vice versa, the giants blessed with
frail, petite consorts. Here the old
French proverb, Les extremes Sc touch
ent'' is verified with a vengeance.

Wales Princess Victoria. the Duchess of Fife

attended an early service at Sandringham
Church. which was beautifully decorated for
the occasion. The King afterward personally
directed the annual distribution of beef and
game in which every employe and tenant on the
Sandringham estate always participates.

usual gathering in Battersea Park. where TWEEN

Tacoma, Wash, Jan. 13.-Seldom if
ever does maritime history record a more
thrilling experience or more miraculous
escape from certain destruction than that
which was encountered by the three
masted British bark Caithennesshire, Cap
tain Furneaux, which arrived yesterday.


While struggling to keep off the rocky
Vancouver shore, Tuesday night, the YES
sci lost both anchors and 200 fathoms OF
chain. The helpless bark was being
driven by furious wind and heavy sea
straight into shoaling water, and so GER
tain were the skipper and crew of her
fate that the small boats were lowered
and hurried preparations made to take
to them.


Almost within an instant, however, the
wind shifted and began to blow from the
opposite direction. Sail was clapped on
the Caithennesshire and she was carried
clear of the shore, anchorless but safe.
Seldom do such escapes occur.


1T was miracle" said Captain
Furneaux land but for the miracle she
would be piled up on the Vancouver shore
to-day instead of being safely in harbor.'

But the degrees Of fear. mistrust. neutrality

something more than accident. Judging
from the attitude toward man when they
see him for the first time. we must suppose
that If they all started fair they would

to note how easily, after unknown genera

feeling If once they, are convinced that his

Religion first exempted certain animals

The Congressional Directory brings out two
rather striking facts about men in public life.
The first is the comparatively large number
with more than a common school education !;
the second, the predominance of lawyers
among them. With Delawares two seats va
cant the Senate has SS members. Forty-six of
these, or more than half, are college graduates
Others had an academic training and only 20
about % per cent.-had the advantages Of
the common schools alone. One hundred and
fifty-nine of the representatives were educated
at colleges and 119 more at academies, while
only 70 report merely the common school edu-
cation The President and Secretary Moody
are both Harvard men. Secretary Hay is a
graduate of Brown, Secretary Root of Hamil-
ton, Attorney General Knox OF Mount Union
and Secretary Shaw of Cornell College, Iowa.
Postmaster General Payne, Secretary Hitch
cock and Secretary Wilson received an acade-
mic education. Seven of the nine Supreme
Court justices are college graduates. Brewer,
Brown and Shiras are from Yale, Gray from
Harvard, Fuller from Bowdoin, White from
Georgetown and Harlan from Center College.
Peckham and McKenna studied in academies.
OF the members of Congress, the Supreme
Court and the Cabinet about 70 per cent. have
received an academic training. Forty seven
per cent. went to college. This is an astonish


ing showing when the fact is considered that
an extremely small proportion of boys ever
get beyond the common schools. While 1t
does not prove that higher education helps
man in public life, it certainly is good proof
that "book learning" does not hinder him.

Low sinks the sun. the robin trills


In ecstasy his vesper song;
With gold are tipped the sheltering hills.
The vale is wrapped in shadows long;
In pasture sweet the gentle herd


Lies down to Illuminating rest;
With shriller pipe the joyous bird
Speeds t'ward the still resplendent


West.


When twilight comes with noiseless feet
The dying day to softly fold.
Adown the lane. whose fragrance sweet
Is scattered far o'er wood and void,
A maiden walks as one who's led


By fancy with her thoughts at play.
Then stops and lifts her dainty head.
And hears a love-note far away.
She smiles, and budding up her lips
Beyond her shoulder steals a look,
Then lightly as a zephyr skips


Across the bosom OF the brook.
The mimic of the warning notes


Comes in clear and mellow strain
That DER the wood and meadow floats,
And gives their rapture back again.
The whistle waits; the mimic winds
Beyond the vale and round the hills,
Until it kindly shelter finds


Within the bosom that it thrills;
With quickening step and heart elate.
An eager youth moves on again;
The blushing maid, with steps that wait,
Comes slowly down the locust lane.
The twilight deepens now her folds,
And shyly peep the twinkling stars,
While now q wee white hand he holds
Within his own across the bars;
How wondrous now unto her ears,
Like echoes in the tinted shells,
Is that sweet story which she hears,
And he in the old fashion tells.
From pure white plumes the locust trees
To twilight give their sweet perfume,
But with lovers eyes he sees


Naught but lovelier, fairer bloom;
One truelove kiss across the bars.


One trustful glance from eyes that


love,


Then mutely fall two radiant stars,
While twinkle all the stars above.

SUFFOLK, Va. Sept. 27.-R. Bannis-
ter Mitchell. merchant of Stony Creek
Va, lured his sweetheart. Mabel Lee,
twenty-one years old, away from home
with the ostensible purpose of marriage
and then murdered her and killed him
self That was on Tuesday morning.


Last night ex-Treasurer Bascom Bats
of Greenville county, and negro found
their dead bodies through the presence
OF buzzards near Callaville postoffice,
twenty-five miles from the starting
point The couple had left home in a
carriage. presumably for North Caro-
lima. and it was reported that they had
married.


Bodies Found Together.


When found by Treasurer Bats both
bodies were lying on a buggy robe
spread on the grass 200 yards from d
road. The girl was on her left side, the
face turned toward Mitchell's. Her
head rested on her elbow. There were
three bullet holes in her body and one
in her neck. Mitchells body, which al
most touched Mabel's, was on its back.
There was bullet hole through his
head.


By his side was revolver. In
Mitchell's pockets were s634.25, gold
watch. diamond ring and bunch of
MaoeTs loveletters.. The pistol was by
his side. The scene of death being far
removed from a telegraph Office and the
hour being late, the autopsy swas post
poned until today, when DR.. Haligan, of
Smoky Ordinary, was summoned.


The coroner decided that Mitchell had
fired the shots which killed Mabel Lee,
and then had shot himself. Mitchell
had about him another pistol. every
chamber of which was loaded. The
horses and carriage were found in the
forest.


Motive Mystery.


The motive for the double crime is
somewhat mysterious. Mitchell and Miss
Lee had been sweethearts several years.
Her parents objected violently to the
marriage. One theory is that the couple
agreed to die together. There was GER
tainly no evidence of struggle.

Jonesboro, Ark. May 10.-The westbound fast
mail train the st. Louis and San Francisco
Railway held up last night about 1910 at
Marsh Siding, five miles west of here, by four
masked men. Information telegraphed 10 ex-
press company officials state that the robbers
secured nothing. The robbers tagged the train
which did not slow up quickly enough to let them
on, and they threw the switch under the rear
of the chair car, throwing II and a Pullman
across the tracks. The fireman was compelled
to cut off the engine. mail. baggage and express
cars which were pulled down the track some
distance.


The messenger was ordered TO open the ex-
press car He replied that he would If the
robbers would not shoot him. The leader of
the gang wanted to shoot the messenger, but
the others dissuaded him, and the messenger
opened the door. The safe was wrecked
with dynamite. which also blew out the side
of the car. After fruitless attempts TO secure
any booty the robbers cut off the engine and
ran further west. Finally they jumped and
the engine wild TO Bono where 1t stopped on
the level track. The conductor followed and
found the engine. He aroused the Bono oper-
ator, and information was sent to headquarters,
the conductor returning TO the train with the
engine. With the exception of the chair car
which brought here by the wrecker, the
train proceeded west.


A posse headed by the Sheriff has gone after
the robbers, who had good start.
