The limp and lifeless body Of Miss
Rboda s. Ritchic, who had been con-
fined to a cell at st. Eliabeth's Asylum
for three months, was found suspended
from the window guard in her cell
shortly after 9 O'Clock last night. she
had fastened her belt around her neck
and Jumped off the window sill, and died
several moments later from strangula-
ton. The doctors were hastily sum-
moned to her side and rracticed artln-
cial respiration for more than hait an
hour. but they could not revive her'
The unfortunate woman has several
relatives in this city. They were notified
of her death last night.


About $3.50 O'Clock, when the nurses
made the regular rounds OF the rooms,
Miss Ritchie was in her room. and dld
not act in any different manner than
she usually did. She. had been suf-
ferjng from melancholia, and was not
considered violent. Therefore a strict
watch was not kept over her, as she was
not thought to be dangerous, and the
physicians did not think she would do
herself any bodily harm, inasmuch as
she had never intimated doing anything
OF the sort.


Hanging From Guard


When one of the attendants went to
her cell about O'Clock, she discovered
the body hanging from the window
guard. She entered the. cell. and cut
the belt which held the body sus-
pended in the air. One end of the belt
had been securely fastened across the
iron bar, and the end TO which the
buckle was attached was fastened
around the young woman's throat. The
weight of the body had drawn the belt
tightly around her neck, and her tongue
was forced out. SO great was the pres
sure.


With great difficulty the nurse re-
leased the belt from the woman's neck.
Life was nearly extinct when the belt
was removed. The nurse endeavored to
revive the woman. but this could not
be done.


The doctor having charge OF the asy-
lum at night was communicated with,
and he hurried to the cell in which Miss
Ritchie had been confined. Several OF
the doctors made every possible effort
to restore her to consciousness, but
after forty minutes, when no signs of
life appeareds TO reward their efforts,
they decided that she was past reviv-
ing. The woman died about 9:15 o'clock.
Her cell was on the second floor of the
main building, and she. evidently ended
her life a few moments after the nurses
had made the rounds on that floor.
There was no outcry from her cell. This
was probably because she was strangled
before she was able to utter syllable,


Suffering From Melalcholia.


Miss Ritchie was thirty-two years Of
age. and had been confined at the asylum
since April 20 of this year. She was
suffering from melancholia when placed
in the institution. She had been de-
spondent for some time previous TO be-
ing sent to the hospital, and her rela-
tives finally decided TO send her there,
where she would receive the proper care
and attention. She was placed in Z ward
whera she received every attention. The
attendants never had any trouble with
here before, rs she never became violent
or threatened TO harm herself. or any
one else.


Her brother, John P. Richie, clerk
residing in Brightwood. was notified Of
her death. and will probably take charge
OF the remains today. She is said to
have relatives residing at a ! Street
northeast.


The Coroner was notified of the death
of the young woman, and issued a GER
tifcate OF death from suicide.

ACCORDING TO the reports received from all
parts of the country by the manufacturers of
all classes of fruit packages in Memphis, the
prospects for both the apple and peach crops
throughout the United States are far above
the average, particularly the former. A can
vass of the situation among the manufacturers
of both peach crates and barrels reveals the
fact that the demand is much more active than
usual at this time of the year. Inquiries dur
ing the past two or three weeks have been brisk
from practically all sections of the United
States. and a number of contracts have been
closed. The best demand for barrel materials
has come from the Eastern States, particularly
Pennsylvania, New York, Delaware, Virginia
and West Virginia, and large shipments are
being made into this section. Another section
which is claiming a great deal of attention
from the manufacturers in Memphis is the
Ozark region, comprising Arkansas and Mis-


souri, The prospects there for both peaches
and apples are excellent, and already large
shipments are being made from Memphis into
that Territory. AS a result of the scarcity of
cotton wood and elm, which are used almost
exclusively in the manufacture of the slaves
and hoops for apple barrels, prices are higher
than they have been for a number of years.

ings at O'Clock. The names are cried in

supreme.

Inc wise people VINO make our
laws and the wiser ones who teach in
our schools have set apart Arbor Day
as a time when the children shall
have special instruction about trees
and other growing things. They
have many beautiful plans and tried
novel experiments in order to interest
their scholars. They plant young
trees in parks and school yards, select
fruit trees and ornamental shrubs for
their home gardens they read essays,
sing songs about flowers, and some
times end the days duties with a
picnic or woodland ramb1e. That is
all very we'll and just as it should be,
but it is not enough. We want one
more day, Bird Day, when the chill
dren may study the varieties and
habits of Our common little brothers
and sisters of the air. How little we
know about them, where they live
and how they live; and yet how dull
would life be without them


What is the first messenger of
spring? In the dark gray February
days, when the woods and fields are
silent, we walk alone, shivering be-
meath the cold, dull clouds, when sud-
denly a robin bubbles out liquid
note, and quickly our hearts leap up
and we remember that spring is COM
ing. Very soon we hear the thrush
call from its hiding place in the bare
hedge, and see the meadow lark dart
up from the wet field with its ecstatic
note, at sunrise and last at twilight.
These dear common birds are the
children of spring and prophets of
summer. They give to the fair face
of nature a voice of happiness, for
without them even May would mourn
in silence.


Birds have, of all animals, the most
perfect organs of speech, and the
greatest variety of sounds and notes.
How many people know that birds
have second larynx lower down in
the neck? The country boy, perhaps,
has heard duck quack after its head
was cut off, or a goose hiss from a
severed windpipe. The nightingale
and some other singers has wonder
full 1arynx, and can shorten or length
en- the windpipe in such a manner as
to modify its music at pleasure. Their
songs are not merely mechanical.
They have marvellous sense Of mu-
sic, and an almost infinite variety of
expression. Each bird has its own
song, yet there are certain notes COM
mon to all, and well understood among
them. For instance, the tom-tit and
the wren sings each its different song !;
the robin and the jay have special
calls and whistles; but when the
hawk scars high in the air above them
and utters her loud, hoarse cry, each
bird sounds note of warning, and
then all is still. The robber peers in
vain into thicket and copse, for all
the feathered friends have found safe
hiding places.


All birds are not endowed alike !;
some have but a single note, while
others have infinite variety of tones
and expression. The richest in dress
are often the poorest in song the
loudest voice has the least meaning.
In the days when books were not, and
men lived closer to nature there were
wise ones who claimed to understand
bird language, and to talk with them
on familiar terms. But, the modern
student is content to learn of them
from books, and very few of Our
teachers could follow the example of
King Dag, who kept flock of spar
rows that talked with him daily and
brought him news from all over the
world. The daily newspapers are
Our sparrows, n d electricity fur
nishes the wings by which they fly.


One of our best teachers recently
confessed that he knew nothing about
birds except when stuffed, and used
to trim lady's hat, or nicely cleaned
we'll broiled and served on toast. In
many of the states there are bounties
paid for the heads of some common
birds, and this fact displays the COM
mon ignorance of the subject. Be-
cause few birds were found HARM
full, the whole species was condemn
ed. The result is that these special
varieties have become nearly extinct,
and the damage done by noxious in
sects, formerly their prey, now far
exceeds all harm attributed to the
birds.


Let us have special day for our
public schools, when the children can
lay aside all other tasks and devote
the hours to the study of the birds in
their own locality. Let them dis
cover their nesting habits, their food,
their friends and foes among bugs
and flies and other birds, the relation
they bear to the farmer, the fruit
grower, the gardener and others. Let
them go to the woods aud parks, care
fully planning their work, and divid-
ing it as possible, some taking notes
of certain named kinds, some study
ing the singers, others the chirpers,
others the screamers, the water birds,
the birds of prey, the domestic varie-
ties, &c. Appoint certain scholars to
write papers about the events of the

about birds, and still others to deliver
orations. On another afternoon have

ish royalty and native princes. and the saddle

durbar will be the investiture and ball in the
old Mogul palace and the parade of the retain
ers of the native princes with chain arInor and
medieval harness. Two Of the four duchesses
who held the canopy over the Queen at the cor
onation were among the large company of fash
ionable people witnessing the state entry. Lady
Curzon also has many guests from England and

Victor Herbert and his Pittsburg orchestra
made their third appearance in Washington
Yesterday afternoon at the Columbia Thea
ter They were accompanied by Miss Carrie
BrideweII of the Metropolitan Grand Opera
Company, who was very we'll received
They rendered a program Of Tschaikowskis 8
Pathetic Symphony and three Wagner
numbers, and they retired with the hearth
est approval of large and representative
audience. The concert was complete sue
cess and promises extremely we'll for the
second appearance of the orchestra In
March.


The audience filled the theater and was
most enthusiastic 1t was seated in such
good time that the faintest strains of the
Introduction to the symphony were heard
in the last row of seats. The applause was
general until the close Of the concert, when
the inspiriting and uplifting hymn of faith
from 'Tannhauser," the climax of the re-
cital, was permitted to pass with hardly
more than an acknowledgment of hand
clapping. But the judgment with which
the houseful greeted the four movements
of the Tschaikowski number and the spon-
taneous enthusiasm which the forest music
from "Siegfried'' excited indicated a more
general musical understanding than is
usual in Washington any other city
where music has become thing of fashion.


The work of the orchestra has excited a
great deal Of discussion here. Last year
it's performances were of very high grade,
and city compelled to forego the offerings
of the Boston and Chicago organizations
felt almost compensated by the two con-
certs Of the Pittsburg musicians. But Con-
ductor Herbert and his men have not been
idle meanwhile. The standard of their mu-
scal offerings has been noticeably raised.
Nothing more delicate or interpretative
could have been desired than yesterday
afternoons performance of the prelude
from 'Lohengrin'' and the Waldweben
from 'Siegfried." Both selections-the lat
tav- haty nrynf tl,ae Z,
opera-require most sensitive pianissimo,
and consequently test the ability of the best
orchestras. But Conductor Herbert's men
met that requirement confidently and
aroused the Wagner enthusiasts in the au-
dience-who fortunately constituted almost
the entire attendance-to an outburst of
applause.


From the comment heard at the close of
the concert it was the Pathetic Symphony,
however, which excited the greatest inter-
est. The work has been often included in
Boston Symphony concerts and was fairly
we'll known to many In yesterdays audi
ence. Its demands are manifold. It must
be performed delicately, with intermittent
bursts of spirit, with the utmost evenness
and with deep understanding of all the
unrest, distrust and uncertainty which
Tschaikowski and many others have re-
garded as characteristic of the age. In all
this the Herbert orchestra generally sue
ceeded. The adaglo movement with which
the work begins was marvelously impress
Sise. lhc SuCCeeulIS dHeSTO movements
took on much color and richness, although
the score, especially in the allegro con
grazio, possibly lacks both qualities. And
finally the adagio lamentoso with which
the work ends sank away in a spirit Of mel
ancholy and depression which enfolded the
entire audience. 1t was an admirable and
impressive Interpretation Of a remarkable
work. 1t might have been more effective,
however had one of the briefer Wagner
numbers been used as the initial work of
the program.


Miss Bridewell sang four numbers-the
aria from Samson and Delilah'' and three
songs In German. The first conveyed
sense of nasal tones, but was nevertheless
heartily approved by the contraIto's hear
ers. German seemed very much better
language for her voice. But Miss Bridewell
was most effective when, responding to an
insistent encore, she seated herself infor-
mally at the piano and sang Rogers 1.-THE
Sweetest Flower That Grows" The song
is unpretentious. but it was heard with the
most tense delight. After that, II the audi
ence could have had its way, all four of
Miss Bridewelrs numbers would have been
in English.

engineer had been directed to proceed
slowly. Water had formed an eddy which
scooped out the earth under the ties and
as soon as the heavy engine reached the
weakened section it capsized and the en-
g1neer and fireman were pinned under the
heavy machine.


One mail car went over the engine and
was wrecked, and Mail Clerk Fernholz
sustained slight injuries to his arm and
leg. Not a passenger car left the track
and 1T was not until some time elapsed
that the passengers learned there had
been a wreck.


The dead engineer and fireman lived
In Minneapolis. Mrs. Wallace is here.
The family Of the fireman Is visiting in
Grand Rapids, Mich,

from the western coast of Alaska announce
their belief that the Japan current has
changed its course in the eastern part OF the
Pacific ocean and is now running several
hundred miles to the north and east Of its
former channel.


Since the fall of 1899, these mariners hold
that this warm ocean current has been
sweeping with constantly increasing strength
toward the Alaskan shore line.


In the fall Of 1899 the western coast Of
Alaska was shaken by terrific earthquake.
Since that time Alaska's climate has been
changing 1t is believed that the Japan cur
rent was turned eastward by stupendous
submarine upheaval, which formed a new
change OF submarine mountains, throwing the
current against the shore.


At first it was cooled by sea-Ievel glaciers,
which accounts for the gradual change in
temperature. The current has finally re-
sumed its warmth and the whole Alaskan
climate has become milder. Last summer
the climate there was rainy and warm like
Puget sound, 1000 miles farther south. The
entire winter has been mild and rainy from
Nome to Juneau.

It was exactly $50 o'clock yesterday after
noon when the special train carrying Prince
Henry and his suite arrived at Weehawken.
The train was fifteen minutes late in leaving
West Point, but this time made up In the
run down A moment later the Prince aIighted
from his car and walked down the platform.
escorted by Consul General Buenz, who, with
Consul Geisler, met him at the depot. The
Prince showed sign of fatigue, his step
light and springy. and he laughed as he looked
at the long lines of policemen and detectives
who were patrolling the station.


An hour before the Princes arrival prepara-
1ions had been made to keep back the crowd
that had begun to gather. One hundred and
forty policemen IN charge of Inspector Archi-
bald, Of Jersey City, had been formed in line
from the train shed to the ferry slip. Here the
ferryboat West Point, carrying two immense
German flags, was waiting for the Prince and
his party. AS the Prince left the train platoon
OF patromen led the way. then followed dozen
detectives, then came Major General Corbin,
Colonel Bingham and Colonel Mills, the
mandant Of West Point. Directly behind them
was the Prince and at his side Consul General
Buenz. Following the Prince were Admiral
Evans, the Presidential delegates and the suite
of the Prince. A platoon Of police brought UP
the rear.


The party boarded the ferryboat, and the
crowd, watching, loudly cheered the Prince,
who saluted and then disappeared in the cabin
Of the ferryboat.


At the New-York pier, at Forty-second-st. the
party was met by Captain Titus and detach-
ment Of mounted police under the command OF
Sergeant Lebers Quickly entering the
riages that waiting for them, the party
were driven along Forty-second-st. to Fifth
ave. and thence to the Waldorf-Astoria. The
Prince, as usual, insisted on riding in an open
carriage, and the crowds waiting along the
street recognized him and cheered frequently.
The party reached the Waldorf at $40 o'clock.
The Prince entered the hotel from the Thirty
thrd-st. entrance, which had been decorated
with the German colors and evergreen.


The Prince and his suite remained in the hotel
until. 100, and then once more entered their
carriages and were driven to the University
Club The only escort for the evening was the
mounted police, a platoon Of which preceded
the carriage in which the Prince rode, and
other followed IL. It was dark before they
started, and the passage along Fifth-ave. at
tracted little attention. The trip occupied only
ten minutes, and at o'clock promptly the
Prince was at the clubhouse.

An efficient and well equipped school sys-

The hospitals. charities and jails have

During the last year % per cent of the

lied and equipped. The same is true of the

Complete quarantine and immigration
service has been established a Station built

same promulgated and enforced


The courts have been reorganized and re-
equipped from one end of the island to the
other. the procedure has been modified and
the time during which prisoners have been
held awaiting trial has been reduced from
about a year to about three or four months.
police courts have been esta blished for

Free schools for typewriting and stenos-

Cities like Santiago and Havana have un-

equipped and in good running order.

text:
From the New York Evening Post


If ii were asserted without any explana-
ton that there were restaurants in New
York which cooked large quantities of food
day and night and yet which never sold a
mouthful to a person within their doors it
would certainly arouse doubt or ridicule.
Yet such is the fact. There are more than
forty establishments of this class in New
York. Their customers. are not hungry
men, but restaurants, eating booths, oyster
stands and free lunch counters. There was
time when every place OF this sort owned
and used its own kitchen. but the increase
CT rents, the decrease in the size of store
property, and the greater economy necessi-
tated by keen competition have brought
the wholesale restaurant into existence and
made it financial success.


Most of these affairs are on the East Side,
and are managed by Germans, Hebrews
Swiss and English, their numbers being In
the order named. They supply roast beef,
lamb, veal, mutton. corn-beef and pork,
pot roasts, baked and boiled fish, fried oys-
tiers. CLAIMS. scallops, cells. fish balls and
soft-shell crabs, boiled potatoes, cabbage,
turnips and beets.


A few supply larger bill of fare, but the
demand for their goods is comparatively
limited. They purchase good wholesome
material, employ excellent cooks, own eff
oient delivery wagons and run affairs upon
a good business basis


When you pass an oyster stand, and
nicely fried oysters and soft-shell crabs
neatly piled upon a platter, and decorated
with little sprigs of parsley, twice out of
three times you look at the wares Of these
establishments. The tiny restaurants in the
business districts, and especially these
which cater to clerks and workingmen. de-
pend almost entirely upon the whole sale
restaurants for their food. Oddly enough.
they can. sell their cooked food to the retail
restaurants for less than what the latter
would pay for the raw materials. This
comes from buying wholesale in very large
quantities, in cooking on a large scale, and
in utilizing all the waste products.

JOLIET. ILL.,, June 3-This city is in the
grasp of the worst flood in its history. All
the lower portion of the city is under water
and it is rumored that several lives have
been lost
The police have the name Of Eddie Nc
Covers, Lizzie Mclean and little girl
named Kennedy drowned.


Several families had narrow escapes and
the police rescued many in boats.
Scores of families have been driven from
their homes and several houses and other
buildings were swept away.


All the principal streets are under water
and factories and business places all over
the city are flooded. The damage to prop
erty will be great


The street car lines are all severely dam
aged and no cars running.


All trains are stalled. water being two
feet deep over the railroad tracks.


Scores of Families Homeless.


Heavy rains, which continued all night,
caused Hickory and Sprong creeks to burst
their banks, and portion of Hickory creek
dam, east of the city. has partially col
Iapsed, sending the flood waters down in
torrent.


Scores of homes have from one to three
feet of water in the first stories.


Mayor Barr has called special meeting
of the city council for this afternoon TO
take measures for the relief of the home
lass.


Many streets are ruined. the pavements
being all washed away.


Part of the penitentiary was flooded, but
not seriously.


Subscriptions for the homeless and needy
are being raised and one merchant has do
mated $500 worth of provisions.


The flood is slowly receding.

canal has been moved eighteen inches out

of the Santa Fee are under water and
Santa Fe bridge south Of the city was

unteer squads of helpers, are at work all
over the city relieving suffering and trying
to restore order.

CHICAGO. May 1s.-Seventeen innings
of the greatest baseball of the year did
not suffice to settle the game between the
White Stockings and the st. Louis Browns
today.


The game was in progress three hours
and twenty minutes. Four runs had been
scored, two by each club. The umpire
was reluctant 10 let the tie stand over,
but the sun was dropping down little
farther each moment and the shadow
cast by the grandstand was becoming
blacker. Over $1,000 spectators saw the
game.


Play on Slippery Diamond.


Nest of the men who had been strug
Cling on the slippery diamond for such
a long time were about ready to drop
from exhaustion. This was especially
true of the opposing twirlers. Callahan
and Donohuc. They had pitched magaifi-
Gently. but toward the last only their
nerve was holding them up.


The result of the game rested with
these men, for they were hurling the
kind of curves over the pan that the bat
ters could not land upon. Chicago scored
its two runs in the fourth and st. Louis
tailed in the fourth and the sixth.


Consequently, after the last run was
made in the sixth there were eleven con-
secutive shut outs, each marked by such
grand playing that the spectators arose
from their seats and cheered and cheered.


Startling Work.

fascinated were of momentary occurrence.

TO one man, but every one of the eighteen

DAILY reeled OFF startling plays which

Liverpool closed I'd lower than yester-
day. Continental markets were lower.
Cash demand here was very quiet.


Corn ruled nervous all day, with fair
" large trade. The undertone to the

wheat had a depressing effect. Country
offerings continue very light. There was
a decided improvement IN the cash de-
nand, and fairly large sales were report

ket closed " cent lower than last night,
purely in sympathy with the weakness
in wheat. Foreign markets were general
ly steady. Liverpool closed 1sd. high

From the Sydney Daily Telegraph.


The representatives of the principal Aus
tralian papers were taken out to sea about
fifty miles from Brisbane in the pilot boat
to meet Nine. Melba on September 16. She
was travelling from Canada to Australia by
the mail steamship Miowera. While the
pilot boat was waiting for the Miowera the
ships company had a remarkable and prob
ably unprecedented experience. A great
gray shark, about twelve feet in length,
was hooked on schnapper line, which
broke. A second time the big fish got on
the schnapper line. and escaped. Then
large shark hook with chain was thrown
out, and the ravenous brute grabbed it, and
was caught. All hands, pilots, cook and
pressmen, tugged the shark to the vessels
side. A huge hook on the anchor tackle
was put through his jaw and one eye, and
the fish was then hauled out of the water.
One Of the crew ripped the monster open
from the head to the tail The vital organs
and entrails were thrown overheard, and
then both jaws were hacked out for the
sake of securing the teeth. Nothing but
the shell of the fish remained, and the
shark was lowered overheard. A rush was
made to the side to see him sink but the
company was astounded to see the fish
make off. First he swan about fifty yards
off on another tack for about thirty yards.
came back to the vessel and swan astern,
and was still swimming when he was lost
sight of. That the fish could swim away
with the whole of his interior from head to
tail and the jaw and one eye gone simply
raised the hair of the pilots and crew. who
had never seen or heard of the like before.

A dispatch from Pekin yesterday says;
The Chinese officials have requested the
ministers Of the powers to keep the legation
guards within their quarters tomorrow in
order to prevent the possibility Of col
Iis!on between the Chinese and foreign
troops on the occasion of the court's return
to Pekin. The ministers will comply.


The families of the foreign diplomats Will
occupy the buildings which the Chinese
government has rendered them for the pur-

criticism of this course among the foreign
ers, who are not satisfied with the fact that

cations. They believe that the event should
pe completely ignored. They say that the
presence of any members of the legations
will be construed as being sort OF homage

among the people.

tions concerning the future relations OF the
diplomats with the court, one holding that
the relations should be limited to the fulfill
ment of the most formal obligatory cere-
monies. and the other holding that in OIL
cial and social relations the ministers
should endeavor to be more intimate with
the court than formerly and should meet all
Chinese advances in the most friendly
spirit.


Many foreign soldiers and a few officers
today violated the governments S request 10
keep off the streets, which have been
cleaned and decorated for the royal pro-
cession. This is likely to create resentment.

The old-fashioned plaids have come in

velvet, in the color dominant in the gown

walking purposes. When well made they
are fetching on slim, graceful figures, but
since the majority of the plaids are very
large they have contrary effect on short,
stout wearers. making them seem both
awkward and badly gOwned.


The sharp line between the right and the
wrong thing can be drawn only by the indf-
vidual A style may be new and fashion
able, but we should think well before we
adopt it for ourselves. Far better effects
are often obtained with things which have
grown the honorable fungus of time than
with novelty which renders us ridiculous


For those who can carry them OF with
distinction. the wool tartans reproducing the
markings of the Scotch clans are very beau
tiful. The original colorings are usually too
crude for imitation, though some gay silks
and velvets employed for shirt waists dis

worn by stylish shoppers, who, If the shirt

for relieving the awkwardness of the big
plaid.

The large run Of salmon which has been
in the lower river the past week has now
commenced ascending the Columbia and IS
rapidly seeking spawning streams on the
upper river. The run appeared above Har-
rington Point on Monday, when the Mil
ler's Sands Fishing Company took twenty
five tons and 800 pounds in a single day
Give hauls), probably the largest catch on
record in the Columbia. A single haul with
the seine Melted nine tons, about i 300 fish
The lower river fishermen are satisfied with
the result OF the hatcheries, and the large
catches made this year will probably result
in several new canneries being erected next
season. During every run the fishermen
have been placed on limit, which IN
creased facilities for canning will make un-
necessary. The limit is highly unsatisfac-
tory to both fishermen and cannerymen,
and they hope to do away with IT next year.

The loneliness of existence in the country, cut off
from reasonable relationship with the inspiring life
of cities made residence the rural districts almost
ntolerabie to women folks both old and young.
The steady strain of this loneliness became at last
tragedy so pathetic that the folks, busy though
they were with the toll of farm life, broke down
through sympathy and the family moved from the
country to the city, leaving behind abandoned
farm The multitude of these abandonments attract
ed the attention of the thoughtful, and reasons
sought for this growing condition hurtfu to
social and material interests Many causes sug-
gested without remedy The heart-wise alone knew
that at the root of all lay the longing for compan
ionship and the fact that cannot live contentedly
in the solitude of the country.


The free rural delivery, giving to the country
daily mail and news fresh from the world centers,
wiped out measure the distances from the cities,
and the deadly loneliness of country life lessened
by appreciation of the beauty of the fields, the
fragrance of flowers and the song of the BIRDS until
the country became place of peace and beauty and
those who lived there satisfied.

gether the city and the country, and thousands avail
ing themselves of the opportunity to be dwelers in
city and country almost at the same moment, rehabi
tated the abandoned FARMS and relieved the cities of
their overplus of population.

foundation stone OF the new Central Criminal
Court. which Is TO replace the historic
Newgate Prison. popularity called the Old
Bailey.


The new court house is near the present

riots in 1850, when the mobs burned New
cato. Many prisoners who were released

Wild and Jack Sheppard were among the

curdling fiction. The last singular exploit

The spunky and stubborn bull moose
has again been ,defying the locomotive
| in Maine, with the usual disastrous re-
suits to the moose. This time whole
moose family was wiped out in about
ten seconds, making great waste OF big


game and lot of work for the section
men. says Bangor (Me.) correspondent
of the New York Tribune"


1t was on Tuesday last that the en-
gineer of freight train on the Bangor
and Aroostook road, as his locomotive


rounded sharp curve on down grade,


saw on the track a few rods ahead three


moose-a big bull COW and calf. He
sounded the whistle, expecting to see the
whole family make a break for the


woods, but they stood their ground, and
the bull, with snort of defiance. braced
himself for the combat. swinging his


great antlered head as though he ex-


pected to toss the locomotive sky high.
The shrek of the whistle sent men
scurrying over the tops of the cars, set
ting brakes, while the engineer had the
brakes on locomotive and tender clamped
up so tightly that the wheels were slid
ing and smoking over the rails. The
speed of the train and its momentum


we're too great. however, to be overcome
in the short distance. and down swept
the fast freight upon the heroic moose
family. There was crash and a
crunching under the wheels. while blood
spattered over the boiler head. and frag


ments of moose went whirling through
the air.


When. few rods farther ON. the train
was brought to stop, it was found that
all three Of the moose had been killed,
the carcasses of the COW and the calf
being thrown some distance from the
track, while the carcass of the bull had
been ground under the wheels. At the
next station the setion boss was in
formed and a crew was sent back to
bury the moose family. The men said
that the bull was monster-one Of the


largest ever seen along the line of the
Aroostook road.


A few days ago a train on the Inter
colonial Railway ran a race with big
moose which was promenading the track
near Dalhousie Junction. The moose
ran for half mile or more at surpris-
ing speed and then. finding that the
footing was bad on the ties, left the
track and ran along in the ditch. Here
the animal tried to Jump a high VIII,
fence, but stuck half way over. and hung
there while the train came un. One of
the passengers says that the moose
looked puzzled and ashamed when the
train passed him.

In the mean time the Chinese soldiers Man

LONDON, April 4-There was severe
fighting all day long March 81. in the
neighborhood of Harris river in the south-
western extremity of the Transvaal be-
tween part of General Kitchener's force
and the forces of Generals Delarey and
Kemp, resulting in repulse Of the Beers
after heavy losses on both sides. The
Canadian Rifles especially distinguished
themselves, one party, commanded by
Lieut.. Bruce Caruthers, holding its post
until every man was killed or wounded.


Lord Kitchener's official report, dated
from Pretoria. yesterday evening says:


Official Report of Fight.


General Kitchener Gord KItchener's
brother) sent Colonies Keir and Cookson
from Vriekuil. western Transvaal, March
81, to reconnoiter toward Hart's river.

carried on running fight for eight miles.
following the track through the bush.
Emerging on plain large Goer reinforce
ments advanced against their fanks, forc-
ing the British troops to take up a de-
fensible position, which they hastily en-
trenched. Fighting ensued at close quar-
ters till the Beers were repulsed on all
sides. Delarey, Kemp and other leaders
vainly attempted to persuade their men to
renew the action.


Fifteen hundred Beers participated in
the engagement, but they had suffered too

west and south. The British losses were
also severe. The Canadian Rifles especially
distinguished themselves, one party, COM
manded by Lieut.. Bruce Caruthers. hold
ing its post till every man was killed or
wounded. Others of the forces showed

The Secretary of State has sent to the
War Department, the governor of Hawaii
through the Interior Department, and
directly to the governor of Porto Rico
blank passports. forms of application and
ports by those officials


This marks important departure, as
until recently passports were never issued
to any other than citizens of the United
States, except for a brief period during the
civil war, when they were granted to aliens
who had made the declaration of intention
to become citizens and were consequently
liable to military duty.


After the war with Spain the State De-
partment directed diplomatic and consular
officers to afford loyal F1lipinos and Porto
Ricans Who were in foreign countries the
same protection citizens of the United
States, but it could not give them pass
ports, because the law forbade their issu-
ance to others than American citizens.


This difficulty was remedied by a law
passed by Congress at it's last session, and
in consequence rules for issuing passports
in the iasular possessions have been pre-
Scribed by President Roosevelt, and the
State Department has now forwarded all
the papers to the insuar governors, and to
diplomatic and consular officers through
out the world, thus putting into full effect
the new system by which residents OF our
insular possessions when they travel abroad
may carry the same document for their
protection that American citizens carry,
and may obtain it without ipconventent
delay.

Traffic all over Long Island last night was
almost at a standstiIl The storm was the worst
that has been experienced there for some years.
Nearly two feet OF snow fell on the level and
the wind blowing at a speed of nearly nifty
miles hour. piled UP immense drifts of snow
in all the deep cuts of the Long Island Rail-
road. Between Floral Park. Garden City. Hemp
stead. Mineola and Hyde Park travel by rail
completely blocked.


Trains leaving Brooklyn and Long Island City
for Hampstead. Garden City. Mineola, Oyster
Bay and Sea Cliff were from three to five hours
late, and several trains for those points last
night stalled between Jamaica and Hemp
stead and Oyster Bay. despite the efforts OF
two engines each train.


Many people from Hampstead and Garden
City were imprisoned from early yesterday in a
train with two engines in deep cut on the
Hampstead plains. and so rapidly did the drifts
fill the cuts that at early hour this morning
they had not been able 20 effect their release.


Telephone and telegraph wires were down in
many places Many oe the highways Of Nassau
County were impossible because Of large drifts.


In several towns along the Sound considerable
damage done to shipping. and numerous
piers were wrecked. parts OF them being washed
away The wind caused immense sea. and
high tides that washed over the lawns OF many
of the country places on the shore.


In Westchester County both steam railroads
and trolley lines suffered. The Huckleberry cars
throughout The Bronx. Mount Vernon, New
Rochelle, Yonke-s. Tarrytown and Mamaronack
were completely tied up while trains on the
Harlem Railroad were from twenty-five TO fifty
five minutes late.


The sorm IN the northern part of westchester
was much worse than in the southern section.
The highways were filled with drifting snow
and in many cases were impossible. In Peeks-
kill the villagers awoke yesterday morning 10
1nd several inches of snow on the ground and
by night more than a foot of snow had fallen.
which high wind had piled In deep drifts.
Trolley lines were obliged to cut of their ser
vice and all railroad trains were late.


Not even the great blizzard OF 1855 tied up
Staten Island as did the storm yesterday. m
that year some traffic kept UP and the
trains were running in fairly good shape. but
were practically nothing. The two trolley lines
were at a standstill last night. The Staten Isl
and Electric Company tried to run ears in the
morning. but about noon abandoned all enort
and shut down. The Midland Railroad Com
pany, after a vain effort in the early morning,
resigned to the elements and Will dig itself out
in a day or two. After noon there were few
vehicles on the streets Even Sleighs could make
little progress, owing TO the drifts. which piled
up six, seven and eight feet deep.


The Staten Island Rapid Transit Railroad did
little better than the trolley roads. Early in the
day trains were thrown from the tracks at Fort
Wadsworth and Arrochar. Late last night they
had not been put back on the rails The south
shore trains were run as far as Clifton or Con-
cord and then sent back to ST. George. Only
two cars were ever used on a train. and these
were loaded to their utmost on every trip, the
North Shore branch did little better by using
Ohio Railroad. These jerked the North Shore
trains through the drifts about every three
hours The Totenville line up 10 last night
managed TO get train through every three
hours.

waterbury, Conn, Feb. 3-Amid smoking,
water soaked ruins, covering three acres of the
handsomest and busiest part of this city Water
bury stands tonight aghast at the terrible dis
aster that has befallen her. Twenty-four hours
ago she was in her fullest pride as a wealthy
and growing manufacturing metropolis of Con-
necticut Tonight, with the whole centre of the
city burned and charred, there is little to make
one think of the former beauty. All day crowds
OF people have come into the city from all over
the State. each incoming train all day being
crowded 10 the rails with visitors. and all day
these crowds have stood the street corners.
held back by Gordon of militia from entering
the fire SCARED territory. Never before has
Waterbury seen such a spectacle; never again
does she want to-


The furious fire that has ruined about Sc OOO
600 of the finest business portion of the city
was still smOuldering tonight and engines
were playing miles of hose on the steaming
heaps of brick and stone. The territory incIosed
by Grand, Leavenworth South Main and Spring
SITS is almost entirely a mass of ruins-a terri
tory including portions of seven city blocks. On
these blocks were the most elaborately built and
the most important business concerns in the
city. drygoOds houses, hotels, newspaper offices,
hardware, shoe, jewelry stores and blocks of
modern flats. Hardly of them has survived
the fearful ordeal Here and there a narrow
building stands untouched but all else is heaped
on the water soaked ground, blackened and
charred and indistinguishable.


Around this devastated area stand block upon
plock OF newly built apartment houses and
stores, saved from like ruin only by the heroic
ehorts OF the hrcmen-


HOW THE BLAZE STARTED


The fire started in a gas explosion on the
second floor of the Reid & Hughes department
store, in Banli-st. at $50 last night forty
mile gale was blowing from the west and before
the hremen had moments notice the flames
swept across Bank-st and licked up as by magic
the tall Office building on the other side. Had
the WIND remained In the same direction the fire
might then have been stopped but il shifted,
spreading the flames with remar rka BILE swiftness
to the great business blocks south and north
taking in the section thickly built up and in
three hours a score of landmarks We're wiped
from the map


NeW-Haven Hartford, Bridgeport, NaugatuCk
and Torrington. and by midnight special engine
companies from those cities were on hand ani
nghtlng the hames shoulder 10 shoulder with the
Waterbury companies. The success of the fire

ot-toWn nremen, whose work was most effective.


Added to the terror of last nights scene was
the high wind that swept the city and car
riCd clouds of sparks to the residence sections
and the fact that the electric lights burned
OUT, leaving the streets unlighted by the
glare of the blazing furnace of business blocks.


To cap the climax. the famous old SCovil
House caught fire at O'Clock this morning and
in an hour there nothing left of this we'll
equipped hotel except Charred and Crumbling
walls. All this morning the hremen fought TO
keep the red hot embNrs from spreading the
blaze, and it was only this afternoon that final
assurance was given by Chief Snagg that the
danger was past.


SCENE OF DEVASTATION


To one who follows Bank-st., the main bust
ness thoroughfare, up from the station the
scene is remarkable. At the junction of Grand

extending for three blocks in front of him and
block each side. Here and there rise black
ened, fire swept chimneys; tall. charred walls,
with their broken window holes and doOrways.
and occasionally a whole building stands erect,
miraculously saved from the general devasta-
tiOn. One whole front of "A business block in
Bank-st. appears to be whole, with not win
dow pane broken, but the entire of the
structure lies in smoking heaps behind 1t. All
through Bank-st. walls We're tumbling suddenly

difficulty that two of the local companies of

PANIC AMONG RESIDENTS.


Last nights horrors will never be forgotten
by Waterbury people. In total darkness ex-
cept for the blaze of the furnace of burning
buildings against the sky, and threatened till
past midnight with the burning of most of the
city there actual panic among the residents
of the city. Thousands busy beating out
the embers that fell their roofs and in their
yards, and hundreds were loading their house
hold goods into wagons and tossing them from
windows into the streets Many more were
rushing to the hills surrounding the city and
urging others to flee. 1t was only when morn
ing came that the panic-stricl1en struggle for
safety ended


The most sensational part of the great fire
outside of the terrible affair itself has come to
be the origin of the fire that consumed the

Miss SARAH SANDS, the oldest white resident
of Annapolis, died at her home in that city, on
Monday last, aged 81 years. Her death was
the result of shock from fall. 1t was in the
historical house in which she died, and which
dates back about three hundred years, that
George Washington sat upon the same chairs
that are there today. Up to the time of the
accident Miss Sands possessed all her faculties.
She read and sewed without glasses, her hear

moist limp chamois skin with which she

whatnot In the front ROOM, the sheets to be
turned and reseamed and the stocking bag

London. March 9.-The Cunard Steamship
Line to-day received the following message
from Horta. Azores:


The Etruria is arriving here. She is being
towed"


Horta, Azores March 9.-The Cunard liner
Etruria anchored here at o'clock this evening
All on board are well.


The steamer had a comparatively uneventful
passage except for the breakdown which oc-
CURED during the dinner hour of February %
When this occurred the Etrura had just fin
ished speaking by wireless telegraphy with the
Cunard Line steamship Umbria After the acci-
dent was discovered the Etruria called the UNI
bra by the wireless method for one hour. but
without success.


Upon examination it was found that the ships
propeller had broken off outside the tube. and
that the rudder had been carried away by the
propeller. The Etruria then sent up rockets
which were seen by the British steamer William
Cliff The latter bore down and was alongside
in fifty minutes after the accident. She stood
by until daylight, when. after several attempts.
she succeeded in passing hawser aboard the
Etruria. The tank steamer Ottawa arrived on
the scene at this time. The William Cliff then
attempted to tow the Etruria, while the Ottawa
attempted to steer her. The hawser however.
snapped. The Ottawa stood by for two days
and then left for Fayal, bearing the second Off
Ger Of the Etruria, TO report the disaster and
obtain assistance


In the mean while the crew of the Etruria had
made every effort TO rig a jury rudder The
first such rudder carried away Immediately an
attempt made 10 use It. After further ef-
forts, lasting for two days. a second jury rudder
was successfully adjusted, and is still IN posi-
tion.


The passengers of the Etruria were satisfied
they were IN no danger. and they praise the
conduct Of the captain and crew of the vessel.
After the accident the passengers amused them
selves with the usual deck sports. and concerts
were held in the first and second cabins. Only
those who were anxious concerning business
matters chafed at the unavoidable delay.
The Etruria reports having sighted the italian
mail steamer Sardegna, from Naples February
26 for New-YorlS, last Wednesday, March 5. The
Sardegna stood by, but, finding she could be of
no assistance, she proceeded on her course


The EtrurIa was hoping to communicate with
the North German Lloyd steamer Kronprinz
Wilhelm by wireless telegraphy. But her mast
wire broke IN several places and she was unable
to repair 1t until the weather had improved
when it was too late. After the accident the
passage Of the Cunard steamer was entirely un-
eventful, and there occurred nothing of interest
beyond the daily runs of the vessel which
ranged from sixty to hundred knots
The Etruria VIII wait here for the arrival of
the Royal Mail steamer Elbe. which left South
/ ampton for Horta yesterday. The Elbe will
carry the Etruria's passengers to England. The
Etruria will then be towed home by the two
tugs which are now their way out from
! Liverpool for this purpose.


The passengers on the Etrura are looking
longingly toward the shore and waiting for to-
morrow morning, when they will be able to land
/ and become acquainted with Horta and the
island Of Fayal.

text:
From the New Bedford Standard


The steam whaler Thrasher arrived at
san Francisco from the Arctic with about
5000 pounds Of whalebone. She sent down
5000 pounds earlier in the year, and her
total harvest for the season, 5000 pounds,
Will mean neat balance for the captain
and officers. The foremost hands and green
members Of the crew will have had long
ride and their share may be large enough
to leave them few dollars after their in
debtedness to the ship is settled.


The Thrasher went far to the north, but
saw little ice there, and not many whales
The bone she brought down was obtained
from five boWheads. She had some expert
ence in the early ice and was detained in
pack for three weeks. This detention lost
for the Thrashers officers golden oppor-
tunity for trading with the natives. The
other boats of the feet escaped the ice and
had cleaned out the barter market when
the Thrasher came to hand.


The Thrashers officers made several at
tempts to trade with the natives on the
Siberian coast, but found the vigilance of
the Russian concessionaires too much for
even Yankee ingenuity.


Gold in paying quantities has been dis
covered some ten miles inland from East
Cape Thrasher people were shown some
of the nuggets and listened to many stories
of the wonderful richness of the newly
found mines. All the trading privileges on
the Siberian coast have been conceded to
Russians, who guard their rights most re-
lfgiously. They are working these mines
and many of the holders of concessions
are making considerable money.


Oscar Whelstrom, a Swedish sailor the
Thrasher, went insane during the early
part of the cruise and was sent home on
the steamship Portland. He sent
ashore in irons at Dutch Harbor. So peace
fully did he behave that his custodians
ashore removed the restraining handouts
and leg irons and accorded the demented
sailor large measure of freedom. He took
advantage of tbs one stormy night escap-
with only one oar, attempted to reach the
Thrasher, anchored mile from the beach
His absence was discovered and a lfeboat
left the beach in chase. In spite Of the
crankiness of his craft and the fact that he
had but one oar, Oscar gave his pursuers q
long chase, and was within few hundred
yards of the whaler when overtaken.


James Allen, another member of the
Thrasher's crew, was left at Port Hope at
his own request. He will remain there un-
til next year and will put in the winter
hunting whales and fur game from the ice
foes.


Steamer jeanette at San Francisco re-
ports speaking steamers Belvidere and Bow
head In Boring October 16.


Herman Hailman, sailor on the Whaler
Jeanette, attempted to escape over the ice
July 1 to the Alaskan coast. but when he
had covered a mile of the journey to the
shore, the fifth mate and a party of Eski-
mos went after him with rifles.


Two other sailors, John Murphy and John
Drew, sent letter ashore at st. Michaels
claiming to have been shanghaied and ex-
to continuing on the whaler. They con-
tinued on the Jeanette.

KEEL, June 80, 1890 a.m.-Emperor Will
liam's American-built schooner yacht Me-
teor, the Cicely, owned by Cecil Quentin
Of England and the other yachts which
started in the schooner race today are at
this hour drifting toward home. The Me-
teor Is in the lead and the Cicely is second


Emperor William and the empress are on
board the Meteor, and will probably spend
most of the night on the water.


The guests invited by the emperor to dine
tonight on board the imperial yacht Hohen-
zollern have long sinca dispersed.


Emperor William resolutely declined to
leave the yacht until the finish of the race,
and the judges and the sailing committee
sent launch to port to bring out provis-
ions to the vessel which carries them.


The yachts in today's race carrying full
light weather canvas, crossed the starting
line at 1875 yesterday morning in the fol-
lowing order:


The Yasca. the Clara, the Cicely. the
Iduna, the Northwest and the Meteor. The
wind was dead ahead for the entire dis
lance to the first mark. twelve miles out
ahead Of the Cicely, which had already dis
tanced the other contestants. The Cicely
challenged the Meteor for the weather
berth, slowly passed her and heightened
her lead. The time at the first mark was
as follows:


The Cicely 3 hours "a minutes 10 sec
onds; the Meteor, } hours % minutes 20
seconds.


AS the wind had dropped a good deal the
sailing committee decided to shorten the
course by one side Of the triangle and to
instruct the yachts to come home direct
from the first mark. The committee, con-
sequently, borrowed all the available steam
launches in it's neighborhood and with a
member of the committee on board each,
the launches started to intercept the yachts
and inform them of the decision before they
rounded the first mark. Acting under these
Instructions the Cicely rounded the mark
and started for home, but Emperor Will
liam objected to this change of the course
because the Meteor was coming on the
reach, which would show her best points.
The sailing committee countermande it's
previous instructions.


The Cicely in the meantime had lost the
FIVE minutes she had gained. and, being to
leeward. she lost five minutes more in jib-
ing. All the yachts with their Spinnakers
doomed out to starboard, then started for
the second mark, seven miles away. On
this reach the wind continued to die away.
The Meteor rounded the second mark a
long way ahead Of the other yachts, and
when she started on the homeward leg CT
eleven miles 1t was almost complete calm.
All the observation yachts and excursion
steamers left the racers at this point. The
yachts were drifting hopelessly.


The sailing committee has decided, if the
Meteor beats the Cicely, to give the latter
yacht a special prize, in view of the COM
plication which arose over the orders to
change the course.


The race of Friday has been awarded to
the Cicely. In this race the Meteor finished
seven minutes and twenty-five seconds
ahead Of the Cicely. but under her time al
lowance the English boat won by one min
ute and eleven seconds. Upon this occasion
M. Guilleaume, the owner of the Clara
which was also in the race. lodged pro-
test against the Cicely. claiming that the
rules compelled her to carry two anchors
at her bow instead of one. The judges re-
served decision Friday because of this pro-
test.

Once, so long ago our great-grandfathers
could scarcely have heard it mentioned,
there lived within the great Forest of Bur
zee a wood-nymph named Necile. She was
closely related to the mighty Queen Eur
line, and her home was beneath the shade
of wide-spreading oak. Once every year.
on Budding day, when the trees put forth
their new buds, Necile held the Golden
Chalice of Ak to the lips of the queen, who
drank therefrom to the prosperity Of the
forest. So you see she was nymph OF
some Importance, and, moreover, 1t is said
she was highly regarded because of her
beauty and grace.


When she was created she could not have
told; Queen ZUrline could not have told
the great Ak himself could not have told
1t was long ago when the world was new
and nymphs were needed to guard the for
ests and to minister to the wants of the
young trees. Then, on some day not re-
membered. Necile sprang into being; radl-
ant, lovely, straight and slim as the sapling
she was created to guard


Her hair was the color that lines a chest
nut-bur; her eyes were blue in the sun
light and purple in the shade; her cheeks
bloOmed with the faint pink that edges the
clouds at sunset: her lips were full red,
poutng and sweet For costume she adopt
ed oak-leaf green; all the wood-nymphs
dress in that color and know no other so
desirable. Her dainty feet were sandal





ering other than her slken tresses.


Necile's duties were few and simple. She
kept hurtful weeds from growing beneath
her trees and sapping the earth-food re-
quired by her charges. She frightened
away the Gadgols who took evil delight
In flying against the tree trunks and wound
ing them so that they dropped and died
from the poisonous contact. In dry sea-
sons she carried water from the brooks and
pools ant mOistened the roots of her thirsty
dependents.


That was in the beginning The weeds
had now learned to avoid the forests where
woodnymphs dwelt; the loathsome Cad
gols no longer dared come nigh; the trees
had become old and sturdy and could bear
the drought better than when fresh sprout-
ed. So NeCile's duties were lessened, and
time grew laggard. while succeeding years
became more tiresome and unevent III than
the nymph's joyous spirit loved.


Truly the forest jewellers did not lack
Amusement. Each full moon they danced
in the Royal Circle of the queen There
were also the Feast of Nuts, the Jubilee of
Autumn Tintings, the solemn ceremony of
Leaf Shedding and the revelry of Budding
day. But these periods of enjoyment were
far apart, and left many weary hours be-
tween.


That a wood nymph should grow discon-
tented was not thought of by Needles sis
tiers. 1t came upon her only after many
years Of brooding. But when once she had
settled in her mind that life was irksome

A class of men who know the real mean
ing of the term strenuous life'' are the
hardy pump linemen who superintend the
transit of oil from well to tide water. They
live thousands of feet above the level of the
sea on lonely mountains. Months pass and
they never see a new face. Clouds, mfsts
and fog, above, below and around them
form the eternal landscape. In the sum-
mer season the work, though hard, can be
endured; it's main discomforts are the iso-
lation and the physical exhaustion. But
when winter chains the mountains in it's
icy spell then the lineman is subjected to
hardships from which even the strongest
man might we'll shrink


Even though the mercury coquette with
the zero. the pipes must be kept in condi-
ton to carry the oil To make necessa nv
repairs the lineman must climb mountains
cross ravines and ford rivers and creeks
Sometimes he must stand waist deep for
hours in snow and water, and when his
task is finished tramp back miles through
snoW-choked and ice-bound forests before
he can reach the shelter of his humble
home. They are heroes of everyday life
these brave men. No one applauds their
courage, no poet sings their praises, yet
they daily submit to exposure and perform
exploits of daring that are not surpassed
In actual warfare The Susquehanna Junt-
alta. Lehigh and other streams whose wa
ters flow toward the Atlantic coast are
lined with the homes of these thrifty work
men.


There are two classes of operators-the
pumpmen and the linemen The first squad

Cool. light and inviting is the very no.
ticeable feature in the faring selected for
all the lighter summer entertainment, the
idea being to suggest to the minds of the
guests. both by the choice and preparation
of the dishes and decoration, the fresh cool
nCss of shady dells and charming woodland
hooks, where waves the ferns soft plume
of green, and imagination pictures elfin and
fairy dainty feasts and revels under the
moons high noon.


Scarcely more substantial than fairy food
in appearance are many of the delightful
conceits with which our summer hostess
enchants the eyes and surprises the
palates of her friends For these dishes
which appear so unsubstantial are found
to be decidedly tasty and satisfying,
though it requires no little culinary skill
and good judgment to produce this result
with such seemingly fairy-like materials.


The Summer Salad


In the summer the salad casts off its
heavier and conventional winter dress and
appears to the wearied eye and taste in all
the gayety of fresh colorings and refresh
ing favers of the new vegetables and fresh
fruits.


The roigning summer favorites In the
salad class are the fruit conceptions, served
as the piece de resistance, and this must
y
ner most grateful and delightful to your


warm friends and guests.


One can scarcely coNceive anything more
deliciously inviting to eye and palate than
a frozen fruit salad, the inspiration of one
who knows just how to proportion the
several atoms that Turk within the bowl
to give the subtle but full concord to
their variety.


When possible, always get the fruits to
be employed in a salad fresh from the
garden possible, tasting of the sunshine,
but not gathered in the heat of the day, I'M
less you can thoroughly chill them before
using.


1t is wonderful what effects one can pro-
duce on eye and imagination by the arts
tic and proper arrangement of fruit. Have
you ever tried grouping the various col
ored grapes. starting with the soft, almost
transparent golden green, with CLINT of
hidden sunshine in their hearts which sug-
gest the tempered sunlight through the
cool, green ocean wave. giving a warmer
fruit and mingling these with the cool,
slumberous shadows lurking in the black
grape. Here and there a green leaf peeping
forth to suggest the old home garden with
its arbOrs and shady hooks. The whole
arrangement is so simple, and yet to the
eye seeking beauty in highway and byway
this picture will give the greatest pleasure
in its restful effect. Chill and carefully
remove the seeds from the grapes and sur
round them with bed of the delicate green
of crisped lettuce leaves and serve ice cold
with the very choicest oil dressing, and
surely 'twOuld tempt one to eat be the APP
petite ever so weary or the condition of the
atmosphere almost uncomfortable.

With the passing of the Black Horse
Hotel there will disappear one of the
old landmarks OF Philadelphia. Men
whose names have become a household
word have stopped at the ole hostelry
in the years that have slipped by since
It's doors were thrown open TO the pub
lic


Some time around the year 1862 the
Black Horse Hotel was built During
the years that have elapsed since its
doors have never been closed, night or
day. For 140 years the hotel has been
the rendezvous of farmers and commits
sion men who do business along the
river front.


When the hotel was built It was con-
sidered one of the most pretentious
structures In Philadelphia. That was be-
fore the Revolution, when the princi-
pal part of the city was along the river
front from PENIS landing place south.
In those days trees grew around the
hotel, while down along the river was a
sandy shore, where the sailing ships
that came from other lands were
moored.


The old hotel registers, with their
pages yellow from age, are filled with
the names of men who were dead before
the present generations were born. The
signatures. becoming DINNER and dim
mer with the passing of time, are all
written in the chirography Of long ago.


The antique furniture yet in the old
hotel speaks mutely of an age that is
past. The high backed chairs and broad
haircloth sofas. with their fantastic
carvings, remain as witness OF time
when society held forth in the neigh
borhood where now the roar of thous-
ands of wagons. trolley cars, and
throngs of people arises from morning
until night.

NEW HAVEN, Conn.,, August 22.-Presi-
dent Roosevelt entered upon his New Eng

first point visited by the nations executive.
The yacht Sylph, bearing the President,
was sighted off New Haven harbor just be-
fore / O clock. Half an hour later the ves-
sci was lying alongside Belle dock, having
made the run up New Haven harbor to the
accompaniment of universal saluteS


The President acknowledged the salutes
from the yachts quarterback. He came
ashore at 1:20 pm. at special landing
constructed for the occasion. Mayor John
P. Studley and a committee from the board
of aldermen greeted the guest the moment
he landed and conducted him to the car
riage In waiting.


Measures of Protection Adopted.


Belle dock freight yards were roped off
and the approaches were everywhere
guarded by police. Troop A, Connecticut
National Guard constituted the military
escort.


At % pm. the procession moved. The
mounted police were followed by Troop A,
and then came carriages containing the
President and his party and invited guests
to the number of sixty. The program pro-
vided for nothing but drive. and the pro-
gress of it took the distinguished visitor
through the slums, the factory quarters,
and the center of the city.


All traffic over the line of march during
the hour of the Presidents stay was sus-
pended and the city's factories and shops
were closed between 1 and 2:3O o'clock.
The workmen lined the windows and crowds
thronged the streets hours before the drive
began. The city was gayly dressed in flags
and bunting. The drive covered less than
four miles of distance and was scheduled
to occupy less than an hour

ing for New Haven on his tour through
New England. The presidential party left
the house at $50 o clock and was taken on
board the Sylph in launch. Fifteen min
utes later the Sylph weighed anchor and
started for New Haven, where she is due
to arrive at about 30 o'clock. The party
aboard the Sylph consisted of the President
and Mrs Roosevelt, Ethel Roosevelt, Sec
retary CortelyOu, DR.. Lung, the Presidents
physician, two stenOgrap pliers and two mes
sengers. A number of citizens of Oyster

First Lieut.. Louis Joseph Van Schaick,

whose love affairs were recently the
subject of official consideration by the
War Department, and who has been in
this country several months under treat

pines, was again successfully operated
on at the Washington Barracks Hospital
yesterday morning.


This is the third operation Lieutenant
Van Schaick has undergone since his re-
turn from the Orient. In November last
he received two ugly bolo cuts across
the left forearm. One was just above
the wrist and the other was midway be-
tween the wrist and the elbow. The
former was half through his arm, con-
sequently severing the nerves, arteries
and cords.


At the Barracks Hospital Major Bor-
den, post surgeon, conceived the idea
of opening the arm and joining the
nerves, arteries and cords. This was
done successfully after two operations.
Yesterday morning. Major Borden, as
sisted by Surgeons Ford and Connor,
amputated the little finger at the sec
ond joint The lieutenant now has per-
feet control of his hand:~~

country under protest. Several times he
has applied for permission to join his
regiment in the Philippines, but each
time has been refused becadse Major
Borden did not deem it wise. The lieu
tenant expects to return to active SER
vice as soon as he recovers from yes
terdaY'S nperation.

Shenandoah, Pa, Aug 12.-Complaint
has been made to brigade headquarters
that the strikers are foraging in the rich
agricultural district of the Catawissa val
ley. The life of one farmer has been
threatened because he attempted to pro-
tect his property and the raids have
reached such superior proportions thatthe
farmers are preparing to take some con-
cert ed action to stop further depreciation.
It is not unlikely that cavalry will be
sent into the district. A widow, who
owns farm, reported that several men
came on her premises and started to dig
pot atoes. She ordered them off but they
paid no attention and did not leave until
they had taken all they needed. One
farmer has several men patrolling his
farm day and night. The foragers do not
confine themselves to stealing crops, but
also take poultry.


The soldiers in camp are daily feeding
several hundred women and children.

Washington. Feb. 27.-After busy day

White House.

denry might meet the presidential house
hold under the, most kindly circumstances.

to the sick room Of young Theodore and
there met all Of President Roosevelt's
family. He chatted kindly with the invalid
for some moments and sympathized with
him. Young Theodore was extremely
pleased with this courteous visit. as his
illness has deprived him of a great pleasure

brothers ard sisters.

breast. Mrs. Roosevelt was gowned in

chiffon over silk with a meteor rose in her
hair. After dinner. the guests retired to
the Blue Room and spent the evening in
conversation and listening to music. There

the Prince The President. Mrs. and Miss
Roosevelt will attend the dinner given by

hung with blue lamps and decorated with

police for once closed their eyes to over
crowdng.

guests out OF the cafes, windows were
thrown open and handkerchiefs waved.

the circuit was completed, when the
horses were stroked and fed, and the
tramway servants richly tipped. The cars
passed each other on the Franz Joseph
quay amid nnroaricns cries


Henceforward only electric cars Will
run in Vienna. These are popular enough
in winter, but in summer they are un-
bearably hot. The lines have now been
laid as near the centre of the town as
the width of the streets allow, but the
dream of bringing them to the Stefan
splatz has not yet, fortunately for the
omnibus companies. been realized.-Lon-
don Telegraph.

miles through the sand, and then the In

American soldiers, deny the reports that
the American soldiers at Havana. Cien-
fuegos, and Santiago had suffered be-
cause of the hostility of the Cubans, and
say that the people of those towns are
greatly incensed over the report pub
lished in American papers to that ef-
feet.


The report, they say, was doubtless
due to drunken street brawls in Cuba,
when the Cuban police had come into
conflict with some American soldiers
who had been indulging too freely in
liquor.


The returned soldiers said that there
were. still eight American companies in
Cuba, four at Havana and two each at
Cienfuegos and Santiago; that the SOL
diers were at liberty to go wherever
they pleased, and were never bothered
by peaceful Cubans and that there was
no trouble except from drunken rows.

COWES, August 5-The second day OF
the royal yacht squadrons regatta was
favored with beautiful weather. The sky
was clear, but the wind was rather light.
There were twelve starters in the race for
the kings cup, with the German emperor
Meteor Ill at the scratch and smaller
craft being allowed various times ranging
from thirteen minutes and twenty seconds
to Sir James Pender's Byrnhild up to an
hour and a half TO the little yawl Rosel
owned by Lancelot Rolleston. Rupert
Guinness yawl Leander, which won last
years race was given thirty-one minutes
allowance. The start, at 10 O'Clock, was
good one, the contestants crossing the line
well punched. The Byrnhild led slightly
and the Meteor was in third position.


King Edward watched the start Of the
yachts in the race for the kings cup with
keen interest and at l o'clock the Victoria
and Albert steamed slowly in the direction
of Ryde to meet the returning racers.


The Meteor secured the lead at the east
ern end of the course and was a long dis
tance ahead when she recrossed the line
at 40 and started on the westward leg.
She needed all her speed, however, to over
come her severe handicap.

| Anton Van Rooy last night made a COM

Madame Schumann-Heink has long been

nounced her as the Soloist for its regular

This announcement occasioned all the

Very probably the great basso himself APP
preciated this and sang with even more

By LAURA KELSEY OENDENlNG.

text:
How swells, with generous 10th, the heart,
When Time tears chosen friends apart!
Then plunged are they, in pensive thought
Of mutual joys, that contact brought;
And from the soul, like some deep well,
There's drawn, sparkling with love, Farewell"
As, turning from his brilliant path,
Bold Phoebus sets in peace or wrath,
Shutting from sight his rays of gold,
Leaving the world all dark and cold,
Friends turn to him, who creates light,
And ask of God, for each, "Good Night"
What glowing thoughts these words convey
To friends, treading their severed way!
What good is done, no tongue can tell,
When true hearts breathe the word Farewell"
Or hear, when passing from the sight,
The benediction of "Good Night"

municipality, who is subordinate to the Rus

Missionary to China Reassures Her


Friends in Minnesota.


Special to The Journal.


Duluth, Mimi, Aug. 20.-Some time ago
several Of the Minneapolis papers re-
ported that Miss Christana Williams, who
was sent to China as a missionary by
the Minneapolis branch Of the Missionary
Society Of the Methodist church, had been
heard from, and that the safety of the
missionaries at the places where she was
located had been threatened and that
they we're unable to secure any protection.


This caused much alarm among her
friends and relatives in Duluth, from
which city she went to China.


A letter has just been received from
Miss Williams, written from Chung King,
which says they are In perfect safety
there; that If there should be any trouble
there are several gunboats in the harbor
under whose protection they could place
themselves within half hours time.


Three hundred miles from there there
was an uprising a few days before the
letter was written, and some Christian
natives were killed, but none of the mis-
sionaries was molested.

SAN FRANCISCO, November 20.-The
Southern Pacific boat and ferry slips at the
end of the Alameda mole, which extends
far into the bay from the eastern shore,
were totally destroyed by fire early today
A large number of passenger coaches were
also burned, and 1t is said that several
lives have been lost.


The fire broke out from some unknown
cause soon after the ferry boat Oakland had
reached the slip on her last trip from this
city. 1t was about l o'clock, and the
kitchen crew of the steamer had retired to
their lodging in small structure near the
end of the pier. Suddenly the flames burst
out, quickly spreading through the depot. a
big building of wood and glass. The upper
works of the Oakland caught fire, and her
captain was forced to cut loose and leav.
her men behind. They may have escaped,
but have not yet been heard from.


The burning ships were inaccessible for
fire engines from the Alameda county shore,
but two fireboats were dispatched to the
scene from this city, and succeeded in con-
filming the flames to the end of the mole.
Nothing else could be done, however, and
everything on the broad extension of the
pier was soon totally destroyed. The loss
may exceed 100000, but cannot yet be
closely estimated.


Inc depot was the terminal 1or Trains 10
Santa Cruz and also for the trains. for Oak
land and Alameda. The depot was con-
structed on fflled-in ground. studded by
piles and was used approach for the
Oakland and Alameda trains.


During the last year the Southern Pacific
has expended many thousands of dollars in
repairing the approaches to the mole and
the wharf proper.


The ferry buildings proper covered sew
eraI acres, and contained the well-fitted
offices of the railroad.

Teacher Tainted Away.


Osseo village was full Of excitement when
the handsome schoolhouse was destroyed
Monday afternoon. The lad who discovered
the fire might have started a. panic which
would have had serious consequences had not
the teacher succeeded in keeping control Of
the pupils. They were ON the top floor and
were hurriedly conducted down stairs. The
pupils in the other rooms next sent
down. Nothing was said to the occupants OF
the first floor, but they had become somewhat
excited over the sudden noise in the hall
ways. When informed that the school was on
fire, Miss Kruger, one of the teachers,
promptly tainted. She was conveyed outside
in safety and all the children escaped without
damage. It was bitterly cold outside, as the
wind was blowing a blizzard and the Their
mometer was marked recorded near the zero
point.


Several of the larger pupils returned to the
building to save their wraps, thereby caus-
ing still greater alarm to the crowd which
stood shivering outside.


The villagers were told off in relays to work
the big street pumps By prompt and deter
mined work, the fire was: prevented. from
spreading to adjoining buildings. 1t was
the men worked all the harder. Being re-
lieved every ten minutes, they were able to
confine the flames to the school building. 1t
was one Of the finest in the county outside of
Minneapolis and was the pride of the village.

PUTNEY, England, March 22.-The Cam
bridge crew today fulfilled the expecta-
tions of the prophets and Won the fifty
ninth boat race with oxford as they liked.
The time was 10 minutes seconds. AT no
time throughout the race did Oxford in the
slightest degree flatter the hopes of the
supporters Of the dark blue. Any possible
chance which the Oxonians might have had
was shattered by the result of the toss,
giving the light blues Cambridge all the
advantage Of station. Immense crowds, as
usual. turned out to view the contest, and
the weather. though showery, was not SO
1nclement as it had been most Of the pre-
vious years.


Cambridge was the first to take the wa
ter. Oxford following after a slight delay,
and both crews padded to the moored
skiffs at the starting line. The start was
delayed owing to the force of the tide MAX
ing it difficult to keep the boats noses
straight. Lieut.. Col Frank william, the
umpire. however, finally got them away in
a capital start.


Cambridge Takes Lead at Start.


AS was anticipated, the livelier stroke
of the light blues gave them the earliest
advantage and their lead was increased at
every stroke. BY the time Craven Steps
were reached Cambridge had clear length
to the good, and it was patent to every one
that they had the race in hand, barring ac-
cidents. Huntley's somewhat sluggish
stroke appeared to be too slow to suit some
Of the powerful Oxford men behind him.


Their weight would have told, at least IN
the earlier part Of the race, had they been
given more chance. AS it was each land
mark on the river banks found them fur
ther and further in the rear, and at Har-
rods stores their troubles were Increased
by the wash of their opponents boat. Off
the saccharine works the dark blue stroke
made his effort, and the Oxford crew strug-
gled gamely, but only for a short distance
Nelson Cambridge did not quicken his
stroke and the gap was reduced to about a
length as the boats shot under Hammer
smith bridge The effort took all the steam
out of the OXonianS, their stroke dropped
from 81 to 81 and the race was practically
over.


Cambridge Forges Ahead.


Cambridge came right away, pulling COM
fortably at an average of 36 strokes to me
minute, and increased her lead without the
slightest effort Before reaching Barnes
bridge the dark blues were In the greatest
trouble, while the light blues. amid hearty
cheers, padded past the ship at Mortlake.
the easiest winners Of the tamest univer-
sity boat race in many years.


The official time of the finish was 10 min
utes 0 seconds, and the distance separating
the two boats was officially given out as
being five lengths, but 1t was nearly eight
lengths.


The spectators, especially the Oxonians,
were not slow to show their resentment at
the somewhat rare spectacle Of university
''eight" absolutely rowed out.

Milburn. This was the first time on record
