From the Los Angeles Times.


From an elevation of 5000 feet on the
slopes of Mount Rainier last week Arthur
Hunter, mountaineer, witnessed scenes of
awful grandeur. 1t was given to Hunter to
view from his eminence forest fires raging
over a hundred miles away in Oregon.
Flames Shot upward from the tops of hun
dredfoot trees and above them rose tre-
mendous clouds Of smoke. AS he looked the
flames crossed the Columbia river, and
simultaneously another great fire began,
sweeping west ward from Wind river valley.
Hunters position gave him a panoramic
view embracing the Columbia river valley.
Gray's harbor. 100 miles away to the west
ward; Puget sound, to the north, and Brit
ish Columbia in the further distance. The
distant fires climbed higher in the tree tops
and then the great scene moved. The smoke
poured high into the heavens and rolled for
ward toward Puget sound and the Pacific
ocean Soon the smoke became one great
blanket which overhung all western Wash
ington, shutting out sunlight and compel
ling the lighting OF lamps everywhere.


Gradually the clouds of smoke rolled
higher and higher. until they finally crossed
the summit of the Cascade mountains and
spread their hot breath over eastern Wash
ington.

Because it was his mothers fondest
wish to see him happily married, Lee
Smith will wed Miss Grace A. Howell
tomorrow morning in front of a casket
containing his mothers body. The step
was decided upon last evening, both Mr..
Smith and Miss Howell believing that
they could thus best carry out the wishes
of her who had loved them both so fondly.
The ceremony will be performed 10y Rev.

Smith is chancellor commander.


Lee Smith and Miss Howell have been
though no announcement of the pros
pective wedding was ever made. Had
Mrs. Smith lived, the ceremony would
probably have been performed some time
in April. but her sudden death compelled
a change Of plan.


= The Friendship existing between Mrs.
Smith and her prospective daughter-in-
law was far stronger than is usually the
case. Together the two women planned
the details of the younger's trousseau.
Together they did the necessary shopping,
and laughingly declined to reveal the
nature of their purchases. They could
not have enjoyed it more had they in
reality been mother and daughter.


Then Mrs Smith died. Her death came
suddenly, with no warning, and the two
families were overwhelmed with grief.
The blow was no less severe to Miss How
ell than to Mr.. Smith himself, for she had
loved the dead woman with tenderness
unbearable.


Last night the two young people sat in
a room in the family home, grieving for
her who had gone. With them was A. F.
Smith. Lee Smiths father Finally Mr..
Smith suggested to Nilsson that the we'd
ding take place before his mother was
buried.


She would have wished it, he said.


The mothers wish had always been
paramount, and the young people knew
their elder was right. They did not de-
muir. Miss Howell realized that her SYM
patty. and tender care were needed in the
stricken household and she consented to
the plan proposed.


Then there was another reason. Some
years ago Mr.. and Mrs. Smith adopted
little girl. The child is now IL years old,
anc her father felt that she should not be
deprived of mothers care. Miss Howell
bravely promised to shoulder the respon-
sibility


The young people will be married to-
morrow morning. The funeral will take
place tomorrow afternoon. The wedding,
Of course, will be strictly private, the
ceremony being performed only before the
immediate members of the two families
and before that silent form of her who
had loved both bride and groom so well
and who was herself so well beloved

o'clock, when another attack came on, more

hypodermic injections the most powerful heart
stimulants known to medical science, but the
patient was evidently beyond all earthly aid.

not arrive until just after the Senator had
passed away. There were around the deathbed
Mrs. Mcmillan. their daughter Amy and a
granddaughter. Miss Jarvis.

OF Manchester for seven years, he having pur-
chased the old Towne estate at Eagle Head,
which he had improved and beautified in many

on the north shore

fected, but the services will take place at the

Peking JAM 5.-The Chinese capital, the
eve of the courts return, presents an animated
and gaudy scene not before equalled in its his
tory. All the palaces, pagodas and temples
| have been repaired and painted to form a gilt
| tering spectacle. The roofs of these buildings
viewed from the city walls, patches of shin
ing yellow tiles and brick. The walls about the
Imperial City are a vivid crimson and the gates
| leading to the Imperial City have been repaired
and gilded. On the towers above the Chen-Men
Gate stands a gorgeous structure Of wood, cloth
and paper, with yellow painted dragon en-


twined about the massive cloth pillars.
Hundreds of Chinese officials clad in furs and
embroidered silks ride about the streets of
Peking, and parties of foreign soldiers, bent


upon sightseeing, roam everywhere. Thousands


of new soldiers from the province of Shan-Tung.


who are finely uniformed and equipped with


modern weapons, entered Peking this morning


and marched through Legation-st


The ministers of the foreign powers have
ceived notice from the Chinese Foreign Office


that all the streets upon which the Chinese


Court will pass will be closed Monday and
Tuesday. Two buildings in the principal street
on the line of procession have been provided,
from which the members of the legations will
be permitted TO witness the re-entry of the Court.
This is unprecedented concession. The for
eign ministers have decided. in consideration of
recent events not to witness the re-entry Of the
Court. This decision is strengthened by the fact
that the majority Of the ministers have not yet
presented their credentials.


Chinese officials have strongly protested to Sir
Ernest Satow, the British Minister against
British officers being in charge all the way from
Pao-Ting-Fu TO Peking of the trains upon which
the Chinese Court will travel They said that if
foreign officials were conspicuous at Teng-Ti
Junction the Court would prefer to leave the
railroad and take another route. Acting upon
this protest the British Minister has requested
the officers TO refrain from making the military
conspicuous. and this request viii be complied
with.


Negotiations concerning the ManChurian treaty
await the arrival of the court. Paul Lessar. the
Russian Minister to China, when discussing the
question of the railroads with the Chinese pleni-
potentiarieS. insisted that under no circum-
stances would Russia consent that other powers
have a hand in the construction and operation
of railroads in Manchuria without first obtai lining
Russian permission.

mines All are able bodied. Not one Of
them had more than enough money for

them were pasted.

immigrants from the Batavia formed

San Francisco, Feb 25.-one OF the heaviest SOUTH
west storms that has been experienced IN many
wears struck this city this morning. The wind Die"

r7evae If reached a rate of sixty miles. Ships
jagged their anchors or broke their moorinss at
their docks a fishing boat was capsized, the tele-
phone and electric wires went down, and awnings
shade trees and fences were wrecked, and peoes-
TRANS were greatly inconvenienced.


Teegraphic communication with the outside world
was cut off. The full force Of the storm was felt
on the bay and the bar was so rough that vessels
were unable to leave port


North of the ferries craft of all sorts were tossed
about like eggshes The violent south wind stirred
the bay into a rolling, tempestuous sea, against
which anchors were almost futile. Swell after swell
pounded the vessels and sent them drifting IN dan
gerous proximity TO one another, drove them close
to the piers and to the islands and kept the tow
boats busily engaged in efforts to prevent disaster


The transport Solace, with nothing but 300 tons
of coal to keep her down. broke from her anchorage
and careered about the bay like a drunken sailor.
She drifted broadside until collision with the
government steamer Albatross seemed imminent,
but she veeered off in the nick Of time. The wind
and the swell caused her to drift heplessly sending
her finally toward the transport wharf In Folsom-st
The officers OF the service gathered on the pier,
fully expecting the Solace to crash into the wharf.
Fortunately the direction OF the swell carried the
and Swung a out into S the Stream

stream. No effort was made 10 land their pas

Mrs. Christophemia Miller is eighty-one
years of age, yet once n week she walks
sixteen miles for a 2J-cent package Of
snuff. The clerks at the drug store that
she has patronized for more than score
of years expect her every Monday morn
ing. and sha never disappoints them. She
lives in the vicinity of Bunker Hin, eight
miles south of Peru, where she owns a
few acres of land and the house she calls
her home.


She lives alone. her husband having died
many years ago. Twenty-seyen years ago
Mrs. Miller came to her present home
from Germany and never since then has
she been on a railroad train. She has
made the trip between her home and this
city from once to four times a week ever
since she came to this locality. and she
has always walked. In the summer time
she carries a clothes basket full of veg
etabies upon her head to this city and
disposes of the garden truck to regular
customers.


What she earns In the summer more
than keeps up her expenses In the win
ter. and apparently she is happy. Every
one in Peru knows her, and she has often
been termed the Bunker Hill fast line,"
from the fact that she walks SO rapidly
and makes her trips SO reguiarly.-In-
dianapolis News.

NEWPORT NEWS, Va, March 5.-The
coal barge Cardenas, which broke away
from the tug Cuba on the night of Febru-
airy 2, soon after leaving Providence for
Newport News, and has been adrift ever
since being carried as far south as Ber-
muda. was towed in here this morning at
o'clock, not much the worse for her ex-
perience, by the same vessel from which
she parted.


The master and crew are well, and still
have enough provisions aboard to last for
another month. but they do not care for
a similar experience. The Cuba was tow
ing ;he Cardenas and Matanzas, when both
barges broke away in the storm, which
sent five other barges adrift, two of them
TO the bottom The MatanZas anchored,
and later headed for the coast, being
picked up by the Cuba.


The tug searched for five days for the
missing barge without success, and gave
her up for lost. Monday afternoon at
O'Clock. the Cuba. while bound for New
port News from Boston. sighted the Ger
denas at Fire Island Light. where she had
drifted. and attached a hawser. bringing
her here this morning.

text:
The annual fall yacht race Of boats kept
at Cumberland's boat house was held Sun
day afternoon. The preparatory gun was
fired at 1:55 o'clock. and the six yachts got
over the line five minutes later in one of
the prettiest starts possible, but few feet
separating the contesting craft.


The course was from the boat house,
around the last channel buoy toward the
Long bridge and return, distance Of a
little over four miles. The breeze was
light, but held fairly steady, and the dis
lance was covered in an hour and ten min
utes. Upon the third tack from the starting
line, the Janet took the lead and continued
to widen the gap of water separating her
from the nearest boat, finishing twelve min
utes ahead of the Scat. and twelve and one
quarter minutes ahead of the Startle.


The race was unmarried by single acct
dent or foul. and the handling of the vari-
Gus boats was excellent, no vital errors be-
ing apparent. Perhaps the prettiest con-
test was between the Startle and Scat,
which sailed almost within stones throw of
each other during the entire time, rounded
the lower buoy almost together, the Scat
finishing only fifteen seconds ahead of the
Startle.

ern railroad, was wrecked two miles south

creek. - Engineer; P. H. Larkin saw that

bumped along on the railroad until the
trestle was reached. 1t then knocked

creek. The mail, baggage and express
cars and two coaches followed, the whole
being piled in a heap in the creek. Ex-
press Messenger Colson was killed. Mail
Clerks Kelly and Riggs were severely in
jured as was Fireman DUR, colored. No
passengers were hurt. The train had but
few passengers aboard. The two sleepers
remained on the track.

North Atlantic Squadron anchored in the har-
Dor at Sandy Bay just at shutdown tonight.

little after o'clock this morning. The vessels
are the battleshps Kearsarge. Alabama and
Massachusetts, the cruisers Brooklyn and Olym-
pia, the gunboats Scorpion and Mayfiower and
the tug Leyden. Rear Admiral Francis Hig
ginson the commanding officer of the squadron,
has his flag hoisted the Kearsarge.


Tonight the vessels engaged in earchlight
practice. the battleships working four lights
each. two forward and two astern, and the
smaller vessels two each. Apparently no sig
mailing was done. The lights flashing continu-
ally over the harbor made fine spectacle, last
ing until o'clock, when at a signal from the
kearsarge, the practice stopped. None of the
officers members of the crews were allowed
shore tonight.


The vessels anchored closer to the shore
than any battleships ever before attempted to
come, and the facilities of this harbor were
never strikingly shown. Captain Hemphi
of the Kearsarge said tonight that he did not
know how long the squadron would remain at
this port-possby only a few hours and per-
haps for several days.

A dispatch from st. Louis yesterday says:
An early morning fire, which destroyed the
Empire Hotel, large three-story lodging
house at 200 and 1902 Olive street, occu-
pied by men exclusively, caused the death
of eleven persons, ten men and one woman,
and dangerously injured eight others. Ten
or more, who had narrow escapes from
death in the fire, We're more or less injured,
and many were frost bitten.


1t is estimated that there were between
thirty-five and forty persons in the build
ing last night and it is believed all have
been accounted for. The financial loss was
not heavy, $4,000, 1t is thought, will
cover damage to buildings and contents,
which were totally destroyed.


The dead: Morris Vail, senior member of

cago. burned to a crisp; lobe Davis, man

The injured Harry Cline, medical student

Hotel, back badly sprained while escaping

About ten others are suffering more or

The fire started a $3.50 O'Clock m, when
but few persons were abroad, and gained
covered and the alarm given. There was
considerable delay in turning in an alarm.
and when the engines finally reached the
scene the whole front of the building was
in flames and the interior was a seething
furnace By that time all who escaped death
had got out of the building by jumping
from the windows or climbing down ropes
made of bedclothes A few escaped from
the ground floor through the front door.
Some of the escapes were very narrow.


Almost everybody who got out suffered
some injury or was frostbitten. The guests
barely had time to get out when aroused,
the flames had spread so rapidly. Some
saved their clothing, which they carried in
their hands. but others were not SO fortu-
nate. losing everything. After some delay
nearby houses were opened to the unfortu-
mates and they were given shelter from the
biting cold without. 1t was one of the cold
est nights of the winter. the ground being
covered with ice and snow, and every one
suffered from exposure. The sufferers were
put in the care of physicians.

taken from prison shortly after o'clock this
evening and conveyed to the railway station

start of the special train which had been pre-

London, March 17.--General Kitchener
telegraphs from Pretoria:


Methuen has sent me dictated dispatch
correcting inaccuracies. His mounted rear
guard was overwhelmed at dawn. Methuen
Immediately reinforced it by all available
mounted troops and a section of the Thirty
eighth battery, which maintained themselves
for an hour while the conveys were closing
up without disorder. The Beers pressed their
attack hard. The mounted troops in attempt
ing to fall back on the infantry, got conf
pletely out of hand. carrying away in the
rout the bulk of the mounted troops and
leaving two guns of the Thirty eighth battery
unprotected. The guns continued in action
until every man except Lieutenant Nasham
was hit. The Beers demanded that Leuten-
ant NaSham surrender. He refused and was
killed. Methuen, with 200 Northumberland Flu
sliers, found himself isolated. He held on
for three hours, while other detachments oc-
cupied kraal and resisted repeated attacks.
At this time Methuen was wounded The
casualties among his men were exceedingly
heavy. His ammunition was mostly expended
and he surrendered at $3.50 a. m. The kraal
party withheld until two guns and POM
pom were brought to bear on them, making
the position untenable.
A dispatch from Pretoria says that
General Methuen's column which was re-
Gently routed by the Beers under General
Delarey was only 600 strong. Delarey's
forces, according 20 the correspondent
numbered 1000. General Methuen's COM
mand at first mistook the Beers foI

March came in like a lamb. Its first


day was more like the list OF May than


the ist Of March.


Persons acquainted with the peculiarities


OF the season that New York and New


England call spring knew that there was .


full month Of winter yet to come, but even


such knowing ones yielded TO the unseason-


able charm of the day. All the indications


were springlike.


Fifth avenue from end to end was flooded


with a soft misty sunshine; steeples and
tall buildings stood out clear through their


aerial bath of liquid blue; every distant
object In the long ur ban vistas was trimmed
with warm color; Murray Hill dazzled the


eyes Of the beholder with the shine OF coach
tops and the CLINT Of metallic trappings


on carriages and harness.


Tho whole great thoroughfare was filed
for hours with movement and hustle. Far
north bristled the woodland wall Of Central
Park In dim softened outline against the
soft sky, and still further north was
DINNER mass Of Quakerish gray, the tops
of the more distant woodlands Of the Park.
The whole atmosphere was full Of that


subtle suggestion of impending change
that comes with the approach Of spring.


The English sparrows chirped a tenderer
note, the song sparrow tee-heed from the


bare twig as IL there were to be no more


cold and snowy days.


The punctual crocuses appeared above


ground with tightly folded cones that in
few days will unsbeathe their hidden cups
Of orange and white and purple. The
| exotic starlngs of Central Park and the


suburbs sweetened the wind with their
, soft fittings.


Wild ducks SKINNED the harbor on swift
| wings, putting to shame the slow and waver-
! ing flight Of the gulls. Human beings


moved In unison with the vagrant spirit


in the air, felt the spring fever in their
| bones.


Men and women went about without


their wraps and everybody complained
! Of the heat. Diana, summing her golden
| skin on her airy perch, seemed the only


seasonably dressed person in town.
AL the watercourses OF all the parks
| lent full-throated voices to swell the spring
| like chorus The Bronx, n yellow flood,


which obliterated all landmarks Of it's
| accustomed course, swept into Bronx
| Park a roaring torrent, ragged in thun-
| derous anger over the dam below the Lor-
| illard house and shot with treble It's ordi-
| nary speed down the narrow defile OF the
| gorge beyond, bearing on it's bosom sticks


and straws and planks and even whole trees
debris gathered in it's mad fight for dozen


miles above


That delightful bit Of Central Park which
| lies between the dense woodland OF the


northwestern limits and McGowan's Pass
| Tavern was babel of torrential voices All
| the little streams that net that part OF
| the Park g,ished and roared and gurgled
| and foamed speaking all the known tongues


native to flowing water
Whoever sat in silence and listened heard
| scarce aught but that liquid chorus, or
| more accurately liquid orchestra, with the
| base Of the larger stream, the fute notes
| OF the rills that were fretted In their course
| by rocky impediments and the thick fast
! coming throaty tones OF the tiny waterfalls,
| which fell in rocky caverns and were echoed
| and reverberated by their enclosing walls.
| The universal cry Of the loosened streams,
| the pleasant warmth of the damp air, and
the tender blue Of the sky, seen through
| the dense tracery of bare boughs, seerei


to proclaim mid-April rather than the
| first day of March


Men watclei TIE skies all day with
ama7 erent and said that cold winds would


come with the approach Of night, but even
ing came with the air still mild and at night
the streets were thronged with men ana
women who wondered at the soft charac-
ter of air and sky. The streets were dry


as in MAY and Fifth avenue, with its soft


electric moons and its host of gliding cabs


and carriages and automobiles and its hum


ming crowd of pedestrians, suggested its

LONDON, October 25-King Edward and
Queen Alexandra started on the royal pro-
gress toward the city shortly after noon to-
day in somewhat dull weather. The rain,
however, kept Off and the temperature was
sufficiently mild to make the day enjoyable
Outside Buckingham Palace, which natu-
rally was one Of the greatest centers of at
traction. great crowd had been waiting
for hours, watching the arrivals and depart
ures and the forming up Of the procession.


There was q somewhat tedious interval
before the appearance of their maJestles,
who drew forth the first real cheers of the
day as they passed through the rows OF
bluejackets from the first-class cruiser Ter
ribe lining either side of the main entrance
to the palace. The king wore field mar
shal's uniform. with the cloak thrown back,
showing his decorations. The queen had on
a straw colored toque and a fur collarette
and cloak. Both the king and queen looked
extremely well. and continuously bowed
their Acknowledgements of the warm well
come extended to them.


No Great Crush Anywhere.


Partly In consequence of the length Of the
route there was nowhere great crush of
people, with the exception of open spaces.
like Trafalgar square, where the London

address of welcome, and where the Boer
generals, Betha, Delarey and De Wet were
prominent among the spectators. and at
the city boundary, Temple Bar, where the
lord mayor sheriffs and other city officials
welcomed his majesty and presented him
with the city's sword.


At the Mansion House most of the pro-
cession stopped, their majesties from there
being accompanied only by the sovereigns
and the Prince of Wales the Duke of Con-
naught and other princes equerries and
aids to the guild hall. where they arrived
without any extraordinary incident.


Owing to the kings carriage being the
last some confusion occurred at the en-
trance of the guild hall in an endeavor to
empty the carriages quickly and avoid keep
ing his majesty waiting.


When the king arrived he looked tired
and stepped heavily from his carriage. The
queen threw off the wrap which covered
her simple straw-colored dress, trimmed
with gold Her majesty, who looked mar
veousy youthful and well. accepted
bouquet from the Lady Mayoress and the
king shook hands with her. The procession
then started off down long, picturesque
row of "beef-eaters'' and the equerries and
generals struggled in behind. Among the
last was the Prince of Wales, who was
rather long In dismounting. He came run
ming up, scarcely recognized and nearly
shut out by the Gordon of policemen who
gathered about the doors.

House Last Night.


Washington, Jan. 4.-Miss Alice Roose-
welt, the eldest daughter OF President and
Mrs. Roosevelt, last night was formally
presented to Washington society at ball
given in her homer at the White House.


About 500 guests were present, many OF
whom either were connections OF the
Roosevelt family, or well known society
people living outside Of Washington.
Miss Roosevelt is the first White House
debutante since 1873, when Miss Nellie
Grant, the daugl1te of President and
Mrs. Grant, was presented to society at
a ball which was the gayest social event
of the decade. Last nights entertain
ment was given a personal rather than
an official character by Mrs. Roosevelt,
whose wish was that Miss Roosevelt
should make her debut much as though
it had taken place in her, own home.
There was no cotillion and consequently
no favors. The interior Of the White
House was most attractive. The massive
mirrors, chandeliers, columns and ceiling
of the east room, where the dancing took
place, were festooned and garlanded with
smilax, maidenhair ferns and asparagus,
trimmed with bouquets of carnations.
English holly was used in profusion in the
decorations. The Red, Green and Blue
parlors also were adorned on the same
lavish scale.


When the guests arrived they were
conduct ed to the blue parlor, where the
presentations were made. Mrs. Roose-
Welt introduced her daughter. The latter
presented charming appearance in a
dress of white chiffon with white roses,
and wearing the jewels which her father
gave her on Christmas. Mrs. Roosevelt
wore pure white, with white lace, and
trimmed with lilac orchids. Miss Helen
Roosevelt, a cousin Of the president, wore
white chiffon, with white satin ribbon,
and Miss Cutting white lace trimmed
with tulle with pink roses. The presi-
dent enjoyed the occasion heartily, and
mingled freely among the young folks.

The house stood on the corner of a

For long years the shades were drawn

lands.


One spring day after the robins had

penetrate every nook and corner of the

The master and his bride were coming

longer.


From that day the gate stood Hospitality
open and the years went on.


One day a little girl dressed in white

hair was parted and the quaint little
braids turned up on each side OF her
forehead were tied with light blue rib
ons.


The child smiled and waved her aand
as a little girl outside passed by The low
iron gate.


Day after day. the two children smiled
and waved their hands, but there came
day when the blinds were tightly drawn.


The child outside watched in vain for

bon, and she could not understand.


One day as she passed the corner win
dow she called to her nurse, See, An
nette, sect"

THE DAWN OF THE REPUBLIC.


Havana, May 1S-The Festivities in celebra-
tion Of the change Of government became gen
eral all over the island to-day. In almost every
town ana village an elaborate programme Of
popular rejoicing has been arranged sunday
here, as in all Spanish countries, not given
over to religious observances. but IS distinctly
q holiday devoted to recreation and amusement.
In Havana appropriate services were held in the
churches this morning, and high mass cele-
brated 10y the Archbishop in the Cathedral,
where the bones of Christopher Columbus were
formerly buried but after midday the whole
city gave itself up to frivolity. Games and
amusements of all kinds were provided the
theatres were open. and there were horse
races. baseball games. circus performance and
even alleged bullfght. The old brutal bull
fights have been prohibited since the American
occupation of the island, but lovers OF the sport
are allowed 20 regaIe themselves with tame
Imitation, in which little Cuban bull, with
padded horns. essays combat with the tradi-
donai toreadors. picadors and matadors The
fashionable sport now is ''jaiaIai." old Basque
game recently introduced from Spain 1t ap-
breaches tennis. but requires much more skill
md activity.


A special game Of ''jaialai." by crack profess
sionals from Madrid. had been arranged for this
afternoon in honor of President-elect Palma.
who. with his wife. occupied a box. Governor
General Wood. himself a devotee Of the game
also was present with his staff. They appeared
in white duck uniforms.


But IL not until the hot tropical sun had
set that the gayety reached its climax. Then
Havana turned into a fairy city, with light
and animation everywhere. The plazas glowed
With myriad cOlored globes. the streets were
Illuminated and the air filed with melody
from bands stationed at various points. The
cafes and restaurants alive with people.
drinking light wines and smoking cigarettes and
on the Prado. the fashionable driveway to the
ocean front, are moving streams OF pedestrians
ana low wheeled carriages containing dark eyed
senor1tas enjoying the cool breeze from the sea
over al IS q flood Of moonlight. Transforming
ne fronds or the royal palms into silver and
The buildings Of the city nesting under the
bigh Wail.q fCrtreSseS. into alabaster.


Two big masquerade balls given by the lower
class Spanish clubs are in progress. and several
thousand persons present at each making
merry 10 the rhythm Of old Spanish music.
PyrOtechnic displays arise from time to time
above the city.

Written for The Evening Star.


Sweet pickles are always a delicious ad-
dition to a menu, especially at luncheon.
What is more, they are usually so popular
that they disappear rapidly and have to be
put up in large quantities. The wise woman
bestirs herself at this season and fills jars
with pickles of the fruit that is so cheap


Whatever the fruit, the process of max
ing is the same, the difference being only
in the first preparation. To make the
syrup after a tried and satisfactory recipe
allow for eight pounds of fruit four pounds
of brown sugar, one cup of mixed whole
spices, stick cinnamon, cassia buds all
spice and cloves and one quart of vinegar
Tie the spices in a cheesecloth bag, add
both them and the sugar to the vinegar and
set over the fire to boil. Skim carefully
and boil until clear, then add the fruit and
Scald until tender. Remove the fruit and
pack into jars. Boil the syrup a few mo-
ments longer and pour over the fruit while
not. Let stand over night, and in the
morning drain off the syrup; let boil for
three or four minutes, and again pour over
the fruit. Repeat this process for five con-
secutive mornings, then seal the lars and
store in cool place.


Pineapple Sweet Pickles.


Pare the fruit and remove the eyes: cut
each one in half, and with a fork pick the
fruit off from the core in small pieces then
proceed as already directed.


Sweet Pickle Pears.


Select good fruit, ripe and firm; peel them.
leaving them whole with the stems on
Drop into the syrup, cook until tender and
then proceed as for other fruits.


Sweet Pickle Peaches.


Scald and remove the outer skin If very
ripe, merely pour the boiling syrup over
them for five consecutive mornings, but If
in the least hard, cook until tender as d.
rected for other fruits.


Sweet Pickle Cantaloupe.


Few more relishes are more tempting
than homemade sweet pickles and no
fruit can be more successfully treated than
the cantaloupe. Pare and cut the ripe mel
ons into thick slices. Then weigh. and for
every eight pounds allow four pounds of
the best brown sugar, one quart of vine
gar and one cup Of mixed whole spices,
stick cinnamon, cassia buds, allspice and
cloves, using less cloves and more allspice
Tie the spices in a bag and boil with the
vinegar and sugar. Skim well, and when
clear pour over the fruit. Cover and let
stand over night. and in the morning pour
off the syrup, boil for five minutes and
again pour over the fruit. Repeat this for
three successive mornings, then pack in
jars, seal and store


Ripe Cucumbers.


Pare the cucumbers and cut into thick
slices, removing the seeds. Boil one ounce
of alum in one gallon of water pour it
over the cucumbers and let stand on the
back of the stove for three or four hours.
Drain and throw into cold water until well
chilled, then boil in the syrup for one-haIf
hour, after which follow the usual recipe.


Spiced Grapes.


Grapes make a most tasty relish for cold
meats and poultry. To get the best results,
select good Concord fruit, and to each eight
pounds allow four pounds of sugar, one
pint of vinegar two tablespoonfuls of
ground cinnamon, one tablespoonful of
ground cloves, one teaspoonful Of salt and
one Of black pepper. Remove the skins
from the grapes and put them in one kettle
with just enough cold water to cover them,
and the juice and pulp in another Stand
both over the fire. Let the skins boil slow
ly until tender. When the juice and pulp
reach the boiling point remove them from
the fire and press through a colander to
extract the seeds. Return to the fire and
add sugar, vinegar and spices. When the
skins are tender add them and the water
in which they were boiled to the juice and
cook slowly until it thickens well when
cooled. Pack in jelly glasses and store
away until wanted.

From the Richmond Times.


Capt. John 3. caves, chairman of the
republican state committee: J. c. L. Har-
rs, secretary of the committee; Robert w.
Logan, United States commissioner, and J.
D. Miller, all except Harris living in the
town of Rutherfordton, n. c., Were one
spring morning chasing a fox. 1t was
COOL crisp morning, and there was just
enough dampness on the leaves and grass
to enable the dogs to scent Reynard with
out making a break. The chase had been
going on for two hours and more, and the
forty dogs in the pack had been making
the weikfn ring. The fox was running
around in a circle not over three miles
across, and the hunters at sunrise had as
sembled on a knoll about the center of the
circle which overlooked the territory which
Reynard appeared to have circumscribed
for himself In his jaunt with the dogs The
music of the dogs inspiring and the
race was perfect in almost every feature
that goes to make this sport the most de-
lightful The knoll overlooked a ravine
about 100 yards distant from where the
hunters had taken their stand. Across the
ravine a giant and venerable chestnut tree
had fallen, and the devastation of time
and the elements had caused the bark to
drop from the tree. Miller was the leader
of the hunters and while standing on the
knoll, Napoleon did at Marengo, Aus
terlitz and Waterloo, he saw the fox come
into sight with the dogs 400 or 800 yards
behind him. The fox ran straight to the
chestnut tree and disappeared therein. Up
to this time it was not known that the log
was hollow. The length of the chestnut
across the ravine was about seventy-fve
feet. AS quick the fox could have tray
e1ed through the log he came out on the
opposite side Of the ravine and made off
through the forest. The dogs ran to the
log and there lost the trail. The hunters
watched them for few minutes, and then
Miller called them across the ravine and
put them on the trail. and away they went
in full cry after the fox.


In about thirty minutes the fox came in
sight again with his tail up and showing
no sign Of WEAKNESS. The dogs were some
what further behind than before. The
hunters watched the fox and again he ran
into the log and out on the opposite side.
The dogs halted again and were put on
the trail by Miller. The fox was gone
about thirty minutes again, came back and
again ran through the log. This was the
third time the fox had gone through the
log, and Miller remarked that every time
he came out Of the log he looked as If he
had been rested and was fresh for the
race. The dogs were becoming wearied.
The chase had been going for nearly
five hours and after the fox made his
fourth entrance into and exit from the
chestnut log Miller went to the end of the
log where the fox came cut each time and
securely stopped it up. In about thirty
minutes the fox ran into the log for the
fifth time. Miller then stopped up the
other end Of the log and then cut into the
log and extracted therefrom three full
grown foxes.

NEW YORK, November 21.-The opinion
gained ground today that speculative con-
ditions had changed for the better, and
that conservative purchases would turn
out well. The immediate reasons for these
views were that important banking inter-
ests were more willing to lend money and
investors were encouraged by brokers in
buying the low priced dividend-paying is
sues.


The tone Of the market was decidedly i'm
proved and the short interest was suffi-

ence of any commission house demand.
Monetary conditions showed Improvement,
and the belief obtained that leading inter-
ests favored higher prices. An advance in
Amalgamated Copper to GO, following yes
terday's recovery, was regarded as an evil
dence of this desire to see prices regain
something of their recent loss.


Union Pacific was readily received into
loans by financial interests identified with
the property, and the stock was quite gen.
orally bought on the inference that higher
level would please the management just at
this time.


Good judges of the market considered Bal
timore and Ohio and Norfolk and Western
as being worth more than going prices in
Dictated. Substantial recoveries were re-
corded in them during the afternoon.


Atchison and the southwestern issues
were strong and reflected good buying from
commission houses. The high grade invest
ment issues were in better demand Also
Pennsylvania, New York Central, ST. Paul
and others all showing a considerable gain.
The rally in st. Paul helped sentiment, and
the Gould buying of Missouri Pacific ex-
erted favorable influence.


The character of the buying in Northern
Securities was of the best, and some atten-
ton is being given recent official assurances
that this issue will take rank with the best
grade of western investments.


Rock Island issues were 'buoyant, the pre-
ferred stock gaining per cent and the
common gaining about per cent

was thought to reflect improving banking
facilities for the energetic operators in
charge of the speculation in these shares.

conditions, but there was little attention

points. The loan item may not show as
much reduction could be wished for at

condition should show some improvement
in tomorrows statement.

The next presentations were those OF
the Ministers and attaches and their
wives and those privileged with enrree,
the function terminating with ordinary in
Productions made by Lord Chamberlain.


Among these were six American ladies'
all of whom were presented by Ambassa-
dor Choate. They were Mrs and Miss
Ermentrout, of Philadelphia Mrs. Fran
els H. Legget. of New York, and Miss
Sturgis, and Mrs. and Miss Florence Pad
elford.


Buffet Supper Served.


When the presentations were over an
other welcome innovation awaited the
company. In the last court refreshments
were not served, and the great society
function was the drawing room tea at the
houses of those presented, where the de-
butantes displayed their court dresses to
admiring friends.


Tonight stand-up supper was served
in room adjacent to the ballroom, and
about half its size. Here a buffet set
forth a magnificent display of plate and
flowers.


The famous gold plate, which hitherto
has been kept at Windsor Castle and only
brought to London on rare special occa-
sions, was on view for the first time since
the luncheon at Buckingham Palace to
Earl Roberts on his return from South
Africa. 1t will now remain at Bucking-
ham Palace. another small sign that
splendors of the court will no longer re-
main hidden.


Air of Geniality.


The spectacular brilliancy and beauty
of tonight's function has already been
suggested. In this respect it far trans
cended the functions of the late reign, but
there is another difference-one that was
felt but not seen. Those present noticed
complete difference in what might be
called the atmosphere OF the court.


The King and Queen did not move from
their places and did not mix with the
company. for if they had begun to speak
to those they personally knew it would
have been too long and too trying at
fair; yet there was general air of
geniality diffused through the ballroom
and supper room.


fingered in Conversation.


After the presentations the company did
not pass at once to the supper room, but
fingered in groups, conversing. The same
thing was noticeable in the supper room.
In the late reign once the presentations
were over those presented made haste TO
depart.


Such haste indeed. was displayed in
the ante-rooms before and after the pre-
sentations that an undignified scramble
was always presented. Tonight the peo-
pie were in no hurry. There was not, of
course, anything like the hubbub of an
ordinary large reception, but the people
conversed and had the air of enjoying
themselves rather than merely getting
through a performance.


The King in Uniform.


The King wore the uniform of a field
marshal and on his breast there we're
many orders. The Queen wore a cream
satin dress veiled with cream mousse
line de sole, embroidered with rose point
lace studded with diamonds, and pail
lettes on the corsage, the train CORE
spending She wore also diamond
crown diamond and pearl necklace, the
Order of the Garter and other orders


The Princess of Wales wore an ivory
satin dress with train of silver cloth
draped with princess lace, which belonged
to her late mother. Her jewelry was tur
quoises, diamonds, and pearls.

Paris, Nov. 26.-When Fannie Bloom
field Zeisler walked on to the stage at
the sixth subscription concert given ny
the LamoureauX orchestra at the Nou-
veau theater for her first performance IN
this city, she was warmly greeted by the
most fastidious audience on eartn
EVERYTHING promised the usual calm at
tending these concerts. But before she
had struck the first chord of her selec-
ton, the G minor concerto of Saint
Saens-the composer boycotted by the
Musicians union of Parls-the plucky
American virtuoso passed through an
ordeal unprecedented in the history OF the
Lamoureaux organization.


Students from the Conservatolre
thronged the gallery and striking mus1-
clans were in all parts Of the house. The
hostile section of the audience yelled and
shrieked their opposition to the offending
piece, shouting Take away that piano.
Their Kisses, threats and uproar drowned
all other sounds. Nine. Zeisler clinched
her little fist, stamped her foot, seated
herself squarely before the piano and
tossed her head in defiance at the gallery.
The noise, however, became so great that
the piano could hardly be heard. Nine.
Zeisler, nevertheless, was not in the least
degree cowed, but continued her bril-
liant rendering Of Saint Saen's music even
While the republican guards who had been
called to suppress the riot were noisily
expelling the ringleaders and throwing
them down the staircases.


At the end of the first movement the
house rose to it's feet and gave the player
a ringing ovation which brought pleas
ant smile to Nine. Zeisler's face. At the
conclusion Of the piece she was recalled
time and again, the orchestra vying with
the public to express not only its appre-
citation of her splendid playing but also
unreserved admiration Of her pluck.

A starved robin was the inspiration for Louisa
NJ AICott's first poem. one winter morning as
she with other children raced up and down the
paths Of the garden in Concord she discovered a
wee robin. half dead with hunger and cold.
which had fallen from it's perch. She gathered
the tiny bundle of feathers to her bosom and.
heading the little procession, turned toward the
house. A warm nest was made for the found
ling and with mothery care little Louisa May
Alcott then only eight years old, fed and nursed
back to life the half famished bird. Before the
little feathered patient. quite strong again, flew
away TO freedom the future authOreSS and noted
roetess, the "children's friend who loved and
pitied all helpless things. and whose greatest de-
light was to relieve the suffering, wrote her
first poem, and called il To the First Robin
1t contained only these two stanzas:


Welcome welcome, little stranger.


Fear no harm. and fear no danger;


We are glad to you here


For YOU sing. Sweet spring is near"


Now the white snow melts away,


Now the flowers blossom gay;


Come, dear bird. and build your nest


For we love our robin best.

open handed. and he. in turn, showed unmistak-
able evidence of the pleasure 1t gave him to
meet the President of the American people
Nothing could have been more cordial than the
Presidents greeting to the German Prince, and
it returned in kind and in full measure.


THE DECORATIONS.


Special preparations were made at the White
House for the reception. Ali the state apart
ments on the first floor had received much at
tention from the government florists, but the
decorations OF the three communicating parlors
the Blue Room, where the President and the
Prince met and exchanged greetings; the Red
Parlor. occupied by Mrs. and Miss Roosevelt.
and the Green Room. where were assembled the
members of the Cabinet and the women of their
families the wife OF Secretary Cortelyou and a
few invited guests-were exquisitely beautiful.
The great East Room to which the Princes
suite the German Ambassador and his staff, the
American officers and other prominent guests
were conducted. handsomely decorated. In
these state apartments. elsewhere, unseemy
display had been carefully avoided, but the rich
furniture and draperes. the artistcally arranged
vases, filled with great clusters of freshly cut
and fragrant American Beauty roses and other
blossoms: the evergreen draperies and the gor-
geous uniforms OF the Prince and his party, COM
bined to make the scene one of exceptional
brilIiancy and beauty.


ARRIVAL OF THE PRINCE.


It 1O:45 o'clock when the escorting cav
airy column swung through the east gate and
passed at a brisk pace up the broad driveway
to the White House. Here at the word Of COM
mand. the column broke into single rank, facing
the main entrance. Another command as the
Princes carriage passed the gate. and. with that
snap and precision which have made the I'd
Regiment famous every sabre flashed from its
scabbard and came to present. A detachment
of marines headed by the Marine Band, had
taken place at the right and left Of the main
entrance, facing north. The first carriage, con-
tanning the Prince Secretary Hay and Rear Ad-
miral Evans, drove up at rapid pace, and as it
passed under the porte cochere the Marine Band
struck up the German national air which was
continued until all the company had left their
carriages.


At the carriage door the Prince was met by
Assistant Secretary Peirce and the German
Ambassador who saluted and presented to him
Major McCawley, of the marine CORPS and
Captain Gilmore, of the artillery in dress uni
FORMS who saluted and then led the way into
the mansion between two lines of marines with
at salute. Walking the left OF the
Prince was Secretary Hay, and following him
came Admiral Evans the German Ambassador.
General Corbn and the members of the Princes
suite. The party conducted through the
main lobby into the Red Parior, thence into the
East Room and from there the Prince alone
was conducted through the Green Room to the
Blue Parlor, where the President was in wait
ing to receive him.


PRINCE AND PRESIDENT MEET


In conformity with diplomatic etiquette the
President received the imperial visitor in pri-
vate and without Introduction. This was made
necessary by the fact that there is now in the
United States no representative of the German
nation Of sufficiently high rank to present to
the President a prince of the blood royal a
brother and personal representative of the Ger
man Emperor.


On this occasion the Prince appeared in the
rich uniform Of admiral of the imperial Ger
man navy, dark blue with white facings. and
rich gold embroidery His left breast was COW
cred with orders. The uniforms worn by his
suite likewise were brilliant. The German Am
bassador wore diplomatic uniform dark blue
with gold embroidery. Count Quadt wore the
uniform Of Knight of st. George a swallow
tail coat with white collar and cuffs and white
trousers and other members of the embassy
were respondent in gay colors and trappings.


The President wore plain black frock coat a
black tie and the turned down collar which is
habitual with him. General Corbin Admiral
Evans and the other officers of the American
Army and Navy wore the uniforms appropriate
to their rank


After the greetings had been extended the
President led the Prince into the Red ParIor
and introduced him to Mrs. Roosevelt and his
daughter Miss Alice After a few words with
them the Prince was conducted into the Green
Room and introduced to the members of the
Cabinet and the women OF their families After
the ceremony the following statement was made
by Assistant Secretary Peirce:


The conversation between the President and
the Prince was Of purely formal nature and
had no political significance further than that
contained in the usual general expressions OF
international amity and goodwill -


The party then proceeded TO the East Room.
where the members of the Princes suite were
introduced to the President The ceremony oc
cupied just thirty minutes the party arriving
at 10;45 and departing at 11:15 O'Clock. When
the party reappeared the Marine Band plaved
Hands Across the Sea-" and with few sharn
military commands the drive TO the German
Embassy began.

London Feb. 27.-The Liberal Unionists. at
the annual meeting Of the Liberal Unionist
Council to-day, definitely repudiated any de-
sire TO enroll themselves under Lord Rosebery' s
banner. The Duke Of Devonshire Lord Presi-
dent Of the Council, who presided, declared that
Lord Rosebery had done great service in dis
associating himself from the pro-Boer element,
but the speaker failed to see how the Liberal
Inperialist party could offer any inducements
TO the Unionists. Men who refused to play the
game and impartially blamed others, all round,
whether Kipling or Rosebery. would meet with
scant sympathy The country not dis
posed to follow the flag of statesmen who had
quietly looked while the guides OF the
Liberal party had led it deeper and deeper
into the mire.


He synpathized with Lord Rosebery's offer
TO reconstruct the party, but the speaker did
not expect that his lordship's efforts would be
attended with SUCCESS. In the mean while, he
believed that the Unionists would adhere to
their own party.


The resolutions passed by the meeting re-
ferred 10 the openly expressed hopes of the
Roseberyites of getting Unionist recruits, and
declared these hopes were quite groundless.

James p. Hanson, % years Of age, Of
Ruthon, Minna and William Friss, aged
16 years, Of Lake Benton, MINI, were
killed in wreck Of two Northern Pa
cific trains at Fridley, a small station near
Minneapolis. last night. The men were
beating their way in a car of stock which
was near the engine, and both men were
horribly manged.


The wreck was a J. head-end collision.
The west bound train had come to a stop
at the station when the east-bound train
rounded the curve at full speed The
Northern Pacific track at this point is
but few feet from the Great Northern
tracks, and Engineer Vomaski. in charge
of the east-bound train, thought the head
light was that Of an engine on che Great
Northern tracks. He dicovered his mis-
take too late, and setting the air brakes,
jumped from the train. His fireman fol-
lowed and both men escaped injury.


Though the speed of the train was
greatly reduced before the collision the
force Of the collision was terrific and suffi-
cient to raise the large wheeled en-
CINE, clear from the tracks. Both engines
were badly damaged, and three stock
cars, loaded with hogs, cattle and sheep,
were demolished.


Hanson and Friss were in the car next
to the engine. which was loaded with
hogs, They were both caught in the
wreckage and badly nlangled. When the
train men reached them they were alive
and able to tell their names and places Of
residence. Hanson died shortly after be-
ing taken from the wreck, but Friss was
taken to the city hospital and lived until
nearly morning. They were both farmers
and were beating their way to the city.


The responsibility for the wreck has not
yet been fixed and the matter will be
thoroughly investigated. Conductor Nc
Largen and Engineer Carr were in charge
of the west-bound train, and Conductor
Dalrymple and Engineer Vomaski of the
other. = 'j,- -

Special to The Journal.


Winnipeg, Man, May 19.-Both the
Canadian Northern road and the Cana
dian Pacific are threatened with serious
dian PACIFIC has settled differences with
It's machinists and has raised the wages
of its freight handlers to the figure de-
sired, but the conductors have yet to be
modified. Some time ago the road In
stituted system Of auditing on the
trains, which has proved very obnoxious
to the conductors. Special auditors are
sent out; they board the train at any
point where they think they can best take
the conductor by surprise and ask him to
hand over everything. When this is done
they proceed to check up the train.


The conductors say the system is hui
initiating, and several who have refused
to submit to it have been discharged.
One or two Of the most prominent con-
ductors have fallen in this way and be-
fore many days some definite step will be
taken by the brotherhood in the matter.


The Canadian Northern machinists,
boilermakers and tinsmiths are out on
strike, nominally for more pay, but really
for recognition. This has hitherto been
denied them and the officials, evidently
green at the strike business, are carrying
things with high hand and entirely
ignoring the mems demands. General
Superintendent Hanna, several hours
after the men had walked out, leaving but
one boilermaker at work, denied there
was any strike, saying the men had SIM
ply left their work and that their places
would be filled. IT


If this attitude Is followed it is very
probable that the road will be tied up
before long, as the engineers, fremen,
conductors and trainmen and others con-
nected with the traffic movement are or
ganizing brotherhoods and will, In con-
cert, demand recognition, and a refusal
would simply mean general strike. "

ground preparatory to installing two dredges.

stream, a short distance above that town.

from the San Francisco m manufacturers. The

been mined for years, the latter having paid
better than any other gulch in the Occur
d'Alenes, as high as $500 a day to the man

steamer Colombia, Captain Heath. which was
at Panama two days after the attempt and
which arrived here to-day. Flushed with their

Philadelphia having moved southwark, the way

reckon with the formidable French cruiser
Protet.

CHEYENNE. Wyo.. April 2.-The funeral
of Mrs. Helen NJ. Warren, the wife of the
senator from Wyoming. took place here to-
day.


Although coming to the capital from far
western state, both Senator and Mrs. War
rem were born in Massachusetts and lived
there until their marriage. Mrs. Warren
was the daughter of Mr. Matthew Smith,
one of the oldest and most highly respected
citizens of Middlefield. and was descended
from distinguished colonial ancestry. She
was endowed by nature with unusual gifts
of intellect and was given the advantage of
collegiate education at Mount Holyoke.
Immediately after her marriage she went
west with Mr.. Warren to Wyoming, where
she shared equally with him in his efforts
for statehood and the development of the
territory. Twice Mr.. Warren filled the
chief executive Office. and the gracious hos
pitality of the governors wife was famous
the state over. When Mr.. Warren under
took the race for the Senate in his first
campaign Mrs. Warren was his able sec
ond. She entertained most generously and
often laughingly told that during that mem
orable February she gave twenty-nine din
ner parties, although there We're only
twenty eight days in the month. While in
Washington their homes, on both Q street
and wyoming avenue, were notable social
Centers.


But Mrs Warren did not confne her ener-
ges to either society political interests.
She was active in numerous philanthropies
and charities. She was a member of sew
eral patriotic societies and was always de-
voted to her church. In the latter she was
president of the Ladies' Missionary Society,"
the everything adviser of its young peo-
pies circle and a most generous contributor
both in her home church and the one she
attended in Washington.


Personally Mrs. Warren possessed those
most desirable attributes of character, gen.
tie. gracious wOmanliness. and with them
she had an efficiency which gave her her
remarkable executive ability. She was an
ideal mother, devoted wife and was the
idol of both her husband and children. For
the past two years her health has been fail
ing in spite of the best medical skill of the
country. A year ago she went to stay with
her only sister in the hills of Massachu-
setts. thinking that thereby she might be
benefited, but the hope was ilIusive After
months of brave struggle, on last Friday
evening, surrounded by family friends, she
consciously but quietly fell asleep, resting
In the faith which reaches beyond the
grave.

Washington, May 9.-With a pomp and
circumstance exceeding that of any naval
funeral in this country in recent years, at
least, the remains of the late William
Thomas Sampson, Rear Admiral in the
United States Navy and Commander-in-
Chief of the United States naval forces on
the North Atlantic Station during the war
with Spain. were to-day laid at rest


Every department of the National Gov
ernment was represented-the executive by
the President and his Cabinet and many
prominent officials of the civil service, the
Legislative by Senators and Representatives,
the judiciary by the United States Supreme
Court and the military and naval services
by officers of all ranks.


The diplomatic body, accompanied in
many cases by their ladies', attended the
church services. The military and naval
features OF the ceremonies were brilliant
and impressive: They were conducted un-
der direction of Rear Admiral Terry, COM
mandant of the Washington Navy Yard,
assisted by Lieutenant Henry George, the
Adjutant General


As the casket, which was closely covered
with the blue field of the American flag and
banked with crimson roses, was gently low
cred on the bier from the shoulders of the
bluejackets the male quartet sang Lead
Kindly Light" Meanwhile the mourners,
the family of the deceased. save Mrs. Samp
son. who was too i'll TO attend, were seated,
then followed the service-very simple; in
fact, little more than the funeral ritual Of
the Presbyterian Church.


As the benediction was delivered the
body-bearers took up their burden and fol-
lowed by the family of the deceased, the
President of the United States and his
Cabinet the diplomatic body and many
notable personases, the remains were car
ried out of the church and placed in a
hearse. A bugle note gave the signal for
the march, and soon the entire long funeral
procession was on Its way to Arlington
Cemetery.


The burial ceremonies were simple. being
confined to a prayer for the dead the read
ing of psalm and music.

small birds, especially reed birds and
ortolans, was removed yesterday, and
in addition to the recreations of Labor
Day the sport of cunning was enjoyed

The slaughter of the feathered tribe
began early in the Anacostia swamps.
AS the first streaks of the morning ap-
peared beyond the eastern hills ex-
perienced gunners were seen striding out
Pennsylvania Avenue and the Benning
Road to where the reed birds were be-
ginning their search for food. Along
the flats bordering the Eastern Branch
from the Navy Yard to the District line.
gunners sought favorable positions for
shooting. Before sunrise the sharp crack
of the guns were heard in almost con-
slant fusillade against the little brown
birds which two months ago were filling
every Northern meadow and hillside
with song. They fell by scores before
the swift flying shot from the sports
mems guns.


Great Flocks Were Seen.


Big focks of the birds through the
morning hours swept over the marshes
and river From side to side and end to
end OF the swamp stretches of the East
ern Branch they moved, while from
every cIump OF bushes and from the high
reeds belched the hail of leaden shot.
soaring the winged creatures and giving
them no rest. Their mates fell with
sharp cry as one and another was
pierced by the flying lead. and the flocks
grew thinner with the advancing hours


BY O'Clock the swamps and coves
were full of men, and hundred boats
were flying along the murky stream.

trooping into John Fraas' saloon on
the other side of Benning Bridge with
big bags of birds. They rested awhile,
told long stories of the mornings

again for the marshes intent upon the
hunt
